articles.title: Henry Giroux on Why Elections Alone Can’t Defeat Fascism
articles.author: Dick Price, Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Three days after the November 3 midterms, Donald Trump named Stephen Miller his White House chief of staff. Republicans had lost control of Congress. For his new chief of staff, Trump turned to a longtime aide who helped shape his administration’s hard-line immigration policies. When Dick Price and I spoke with Henry A. Giroux, LA Progressive’s associate editor and a scholar of critical pedagogy at McMaster University, we wanted to know what Democrats could do with the opening voters had given them. Giroux had just taken up Miller’s promotion in his LA Progressive essay, “Trump’s Revenge Presidency: Stephen Miller and the Machinery of State Terror.” “Elections don’t defeat fascism,” Giroux told us. He welcomed the Democratic gains and the chance to limit the damage the administration could do. He also saw Miller’s promotion as a sign that Trump would double down in the face of an electoral rebuke. If voters had repudiated the administration, what would it take to challenge the conditions that had made its politics possible? Who feels the harm first? Giroux sees Miller as an architect of a governing project that brings together white nationalism, concentrated economic power, and the use of cruelty as a political tool. He traced its American roots through slavery, the dispossession of Indigenous peoples, and Jim Crow. Those histories, he argued, help explain how a society learns to accept the use of state power against some groups as an ordinary part of public life. I asked Henry how people come to recognize a system whose harms they experience so differently. Schooling is one form of education. People also learn from what happens to them and to those they love. People closest to exploitation often understand its workings through years of dealing with it. Those whose circumstances insulate them may begin to recognize the danger only when it reaches them. By then, the people who have been living with it all along have already paid a steep price. Giroux pushed back against the pessimism in my question. He spoke about people who had approached him after public talks and thanked him for giving them language for what they were living through. They could use that language to connect what they had been left to handle alone with decisions about whose needs count and who has the power to make those decisions. “The juice is in the connections,” he said. He sees neighborhoods, workplaces, classrooms, and movements as places where people can make those connections together. In his view, education becomes democratic when it helps people identify who holds power and gives them ways to hold that power accountable. He also argued that a media environment dominated by billionaires can flood people with information and still leave them with little sense of how one event connects to the next. For independent media and organizers, he said, the work is to tell a story that makes those relationships visible and gives people a way to imagine a society organized around different priorities. Related: Trump’s Revenge Presidency: Stephen Miller and the Machinery of State Terror What an affordability campaign can leave out Dick asked whether the midterm results also reflected a moral revulsion. The price of eggs and gasoline mattered. He thought voters could also have been responding to the brutality they saw in immigration enforcement, the suffering in Gaza, and the contempt Trump and Miller brought to public life. How could that revulsion become a movement capable of changing the institutions that had enabled those policies? Giroux welcomed campaigns that spoke to the cost of groceries and health care. His concern was what an agenda organized around affordability might leave untouched. A family can get some relief at the checkout counter while still facing racial discrimination, insecure work, or a political system that gives wealthy donors more influence than the people who live with the consequences. Affordability asks whether people can pay their bills. A democratic politics has to ask who has the power to shape the terms on which people work, live, and raise their children. That is where my longtime argument with Dick about the two major parties came back into the conversation. I have watched both parties court deep-pocketed interests while inequality grows. The November results give Democrats a chance to show whose interests they will serve when they have the power to set an agenda. That means looking at their votes, their donors, and what they are prepared to do when the two come into conflict. Related: Two Moralities, Two Futures: Youth in Revolt Against Gangster Capitalism What to do with the opening When I asked what people could do now, Giroux started with the promises candidates made to voters. Take those promises seriously, he said, and hold elected officials to them. He called for public scrutiny of campaign money, including support from pro-Israel groups such as AIPAC, and for organizing that can continue between elections. He pointed to mass protest, labor organizing, and strikes as ways people can exercise power together. There is a place for immediate reforms in that work. Giroux said he would support measures that protect people from being harmed now. His longer-term aim is what he called socialist democracy, which would require rebuilding institutions and shifting power toward the people whose lives are shaped by their decisions. For me, that is a test of whether we are serious about building a multiracial democracy. The people who have lived longest with racial exclusion and economic exploitation bring knowledge that should shape what gets built. How much democratic power we gain from this election will depend in part on whether those communities can set the agenda and hold the people elected in November to it.

articles.title: Compare Nic Salt Deals
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Nic salt offers can look deceptively simple: a multi-buy price, a percentage discount, perhaps a “buy three, get one free” message. Yet the cheapest-looking option is not always the best value—or even the right product for your device and preferences. That matters because nicotine salts are not interchangeable in the way many shoppers assume. Two bottles may have the same listed nicotine strength and flavour name, but differ in bottle size, VG/PG ratio, formula, coil compatibility, batch freshness, and the quality of information available before purchase. A deal only makes sense when the products being compared are genuinely equivalent. The most reliable approach is to slow down just enough to compare the details that affect use, not merely the headline price. Whether you are stocking up on familiar favourites or trying a new range, a few checks can prevent wasted bottles and disappointing purchases. Start by Comparing Like With Like The first rule is straightforward: compare nicotine salts by total volume, nicotine strength, and intended device type before looking at the discount. In the UK, nicotine-containing e-liquid is generally sold in 10ml bottles under TPD rules. That makes price comparisons easier, but there are still differences worth noting. A deal containing four 10ml bottles at 10mg/ml is not directly comparable with four bottles at 20mg/ml if your usual preference is 10mg. The higher-strength bundle may be cheaper per bottle, but it is not necessarily useful to you. Similarly, consider whether the offer lets you mix flavours and strengths. A fixed bundle of five bottles might be good value in theory, but less so if it includes flavours you would not normally choose. The best multi-buy arrangements give you flexibility without requiring you to overcommit to one profile. Check Nicotine Strength and Formula Nic salts are typically available in strengths such as 5mg, 10mg, and 20mg. The right choice depends on individual nicotine needs, device output, and vaping habits. More nicotine is not automatically better value; it may simply be unsuitable for the way you vape. It is also useful to distinguish between standard nicotine salts and products marketed as “hybrid” blends. Some e-liquids combine freebase nicotine and nicotine salts, which can alter throat sensation and perceived delivery. If you know that a particular format works for you, make sure a promotional listing does not obscure a formula change behind similar packaging or flavour names. Treat the Product Page as a Specification Sheet A good nic salt comparison involves reading beyond the collection page. Product listings should make it easy to confirm the essentials: nicotine strength, bottle capacity, VG/PG ratio, ingredients, flavour description, and suitability for a specific type of kit. For example, a 50/50 VG/PG ratio is common for nic salts because it generally performs well in lower-powered pod kits and starter devices. But that does not mean every 50/50 liquid will feel identical. Sweeteners, cooling agents, and flavour concentrates can affect coil life and day-to-day enjoyment. When reviewing a retailer’s range, a well-organised category page such as Washington Vapes UK can be useful for checking available brands, strengths, and formats in one place. The important point is not to stop at the deal banner: open the individual product information and confirm that the bottles match your device and usual requirements. Look for Details That Are Easy to Miss Certain practical details are often overlooked when shoppers focus on price: ● Whether the liquid is designed for mouth-to-lung pods rather than high-wattage sub-ohm tanks ● The stated VG/PG ratio and whether your coils handle it well ● The country of manufacture and visible regulatory information ● Expiry or best-before guidance, where supplied ● Whether “ice,” “cool,” or “fresh” in the flavour name indicates a strong cooling effect These factors can influence whether you finish the bottle, need to replace coils more often, or find the flavour comfortable to vape regularly. Calculate the Real Cost Per Bottle Once you have confirmed that the products are comparable, do the basic maths. Divide the total bundle price by the number of bottles you will realistically use. Then factor in delivery charges, thresholds for free delivery, and any discount code restrictions. A £10 offer for five bottles is effectively £2 per bottle—unless delivery adds £3.99 and you only wanted two of those flavours. In that case, buying a smaller selection from a retailer with lower delivery costs may be the more economical choice. It is also worth separating genuine multi-buy pricing from temporary percentage-off promotions. A “20% off” offer can sound substantial, but a competing store may have a lower regular price. Compare the final basket total rather than the claimed saving. Consider Freshness, Choice, and Coil Impact Value is not only about the amount paid at checkout. Buying more e-liquid than you can comfortably use before it degrades is false economy. Nic salts are generally stable when stored properly—away from heat, direct sunlight, and air exposure—but flavour can fade over time, especially once bottles are opened. Choice matters for another reason: flavour fatigue. Ordering five bottles of one flavour may seem efficient, yet many vapers prefer alternating between fruit, tobacco, menthol, or dessert profiles. A mixed bundle reduces the risk of being left with several unopened bottles you no longer want. Finally, think about coil performance. Very sweet liquids can be enjoyable, but they may darken and caramelise on coils more quickly than cleaner flavour profiles. If a low-cost bundle leads to more frequent pod or coil replacements, the apparent saving can disappear. Make Deals Work for Your Actual Routine The smartest nic salt deal is usually not the largest one. It is the one that fits your strength preference, device, flavour habits, and budget without creating waste. Before checking out, ask three simple questions: Would I choose these exact bottles at their normal price? Will they work in my current kit? And is the final cost genuinely lower after delivery and any exclusions? If the answer is yes, the deal is probably worth taking. If not, a smaller order—or waiting for a more flexible multi-buy—may be the better decision. Nicotine is addictive, so products should always be used responsibly and kept out of reach of children and pets.

articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Jackpot slots offer a thrilling blend of chance and strategy, often featuring progressive prizes that grow with every spin. Fortunately, you don’t need to wager real money to experience these games. Many platforms provide free versions of jackpot-style slots, allowing players to explore their mechanics and excitement risk-free. Choosing Jackpot Slots by Features and Play Modes When selecting jackpot slots, prioritize games with clearly defined bonus mechanics. Tips for Spotting New Jackpot Releases New jackpot slots often debut in “New” or “Featured” sections within the lobby, where they receive prominent placement. Utilize lobby filters to quickly locate fresh jackpot titles and follow site news or blogs for announcements about upcoming releases or limited-time events. Engaging with new games early maximizes your chances of experiencing full jackpot features and bonus rounds before they become widely played. Managing Play Sessions Effectively Setting clear session goals enhances your jackpot slot experience. Start with short sessions focused on understanding a game’s bonus rhythm and jackpot triggers. Rotate between a few favorites to compare feature pacing and jackpot frequency, which helps identify which titles align with your style. Decide beforehand whether you want to explore new games or commit to extended play on proven favorites. This approach prevents fatigue and keeps gameplay rewarding. articles.title: Voter Guide Style:
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A ranking looks like a fact. Number one sits at the top, number twelve sits below it, and the order feels settled. It is closer to a poll, an opinion with data attached, and it deserves the same questions a careful voter asks of any survey: who built it, with what assumptions, and how sure are they? With Week 10 of the NFL season arriving, plenty of fantasy managers are leaning on fantasy football rankings to decide who starts and who sits. The board RotoWire publishes is a useful example because it states its method plainly: a weekly consensus from named analysts, filterable by scoring format. That is the kind of transparency worth looking for anywhere, and the rest of this guide shows how to use it. Where rankings come from Every ranking starts with a projection, and every projection starts with assumptions. An analyst estimates how many touches a player will get, converts that into points under a particular scoring system, and then adjusts for matchup, health and game script. Each step contains a judgment call. Some of the inputs are evidence. Snap counts and last month's box scores are records of what happened. Others are interpretation: whether a running back's sore ankle will cost him a quarter of work, whether a new offensive coordinator will pass more, whether a quiet three weeks was a slump or the new normal. Two honest analysts can read the same numbers and finish a few spots apart. That gap is the first lesson. A player ranked eighth by one expert and fourteenth by another is not a contradiction. It is a range, and the range tells you more about risk than either single number does. Dates matter too. An injury report that changed on Saturday can make Friday's list stale, so check the timestamp before trusting the order. Reading the 2026 board under your own rules Rankings are written for an average league, and few leagues are average. Full point per reception formats lift pass catchers, while standard scoring rewards backs who carry the ball, with half point leagues landing between the two. RotoWire's board, which carried a November 9 update date when this piece was prepared, lets readers switch between them, and the order shifts as they do. Superflex leagues and dynasty leagues have their own versions again. So the practical method is short. Pick the list that matches your league settings. Look at the update date and the experts behind it. Then compare two or three players you are actually deciding between, instead of scrolling for the biggest name. The list is a starting point, not a forecast of certain results, and a rest of season board in mid November answers a different question from a preseason draft sheet. Also compare ranking with ADP, the average draft position that shows where players were really selected. When the two disagree sharply, someone is making a claim worth understanding before acting on it. Cutting through hype Fantasy media runs on confidence, and the loudest claim is rarely the best supported one. The same habits that help readers survive an election season work here. Compare at least two sources before a big move. Ask whether a bold take rests on one big game or on a pattern across months. Notice who profits when you believe it, since a sponsored pick and an independent one deserve different weight. Selective evidence is the most common trick. A player "has scored in six straight weeks" sounds decisive until you learn the streak began against the league's weakest defenses. A rookie described as "unstoppable" may have played eleven snaps. Good analysis shows its denominator. Readers of LA Progressive will recognize the pattern from political coverage, where one cherry picked statistic can carry a whole argument. Skepticism is a transferable skill, though it has limits: being sharp about a ballot measure does not prove anyone is sharp about a wide receiver, and nobody's politics predict their waiver wire. The useful part is the method, not the ideology. Keeping fantasy in perspective Most fantasy football is free, and it is at its best that way: a group chat, a worthless trophy and a season of low stakes arguments. Free leagues are the safest place to test how much weight a ranking deserves. Some leagues and contests involve money, and availability varies by state, so anyone considering paid play should confirm the rules where they live, and paid participation is for adults 21 and over. Sports betting is a separate activity from fantasy and is legal only in certain states. If money is involved, set a time limit and a spending limit before the season starts, and treat both as fixed. No ranking is financial advice, and a high ranked player does not guarantee a return. If paid play stops being enjoyable, the National Council on Problem Gambling offers guidance and a national helpline, with details at 1800myreset.org. The takeaway Question the method, compare the evidence and accept that uncertainty never leaves the list. The best managers are not the ones who find the one true ranking. They are the ones who know what each list assumes and adjust when their own league says otherwise. If you do play for money, play responsibly and never chase losses.

articles.title: Read an IPO Prospectus
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. An initial public offering prospectus can look intimidating. Hundreds of pages may cover financial statements, risk factors, legal disclosures, ownership tables, executive compensation, and details about how shares will be sold. Yet investors do not need to memorize every line to understand what the document is trying to reveal. A disciplined reading process can separate the most decision-useful information from the boilerplate and help readers understand how a private company expects to operate under public-market scrutiny. What an IPO Prospectus is Designed to Do A prospectus is primarily a disclosure document. It explains the company, the securities being offered, the major risks management has identified, and the financial information available to prospective investors. It is not a marketing brochure, even though the company naturally presents its business model and opportunity. The document is also not a guarantee that every risk is equally likely. Its value comes from showing what management, advisers, and regulators consider material enough to disclose before shares begin public trading. Start with the Business Model, not the Headline Valuation Before focusing on price, readers should understand how the company makes money. Key questions include who pays the company, what customers are buying, how recurring the revenue is, and whether a small number of customers account for a large share of sales. In fast-growing technology businesses, reported revenue growth can be impressive while the underlying economics are still developing. Understanding the product, customer base, and cost structure provides context for every later section of the filing. For a company approaching the public markets, a resource tracking the Anthropic IPO can be useful as a reference point while reading the filing and following the listing process. The key is to treat the market page and the prospectus as complementary sources rather than substitutes for one another. Read Risk Factors for Concentration, Dependence, and Execution Risk Risk-factor sections are often long because companies must describe a wide range of adverse outcomes. Rather than treating every paragraph equally, look for repeated themes. Dependence on a small number of suppliers, customers, cloud providers, distribution partners, or key executives may matter more than generic language about competition. The same is true for regulatory exposure, intellectual-property disputes, cybersecurity obligations, and the cost of expanding into new markets. Repetition often signals which uncertainties are most central to the business model. Use the Financial Statements to Test the Narrative The income statement, balance sheet, and cash-flow statement provide a way to test the story told elsewhere in the document. Revenue growth alone does not show whether a business is becoming more efficient. Readers can also examine gross margin, operating expenses, cash consumption, capital requirements, and the relationship between reported earnings and cash flow. A company can grow quickly while requiring substantial outside capital, and that distinction can shape how investors think about future financing needs. Pay Attention to Dilution and Ownership The capitalization and ownership sections explain who owns the company before the offering and how that ownership may change afterward. New shares issued in an IPO can dilute existing holders, while employee options, restricted stock units, convertible securities, or other instruments may create additional future dilution. Voting control can also remain concentrated even after a company becomes public. These details matter because economic ownership and decision-making power are not always distributed in the same way. Look at Use of Proceeds The use-of-proceeds section explains what the company expects to do with the money raised. Proceeds may fund research, hiring, infrastructure, acquisitions, debt repayment, or general corporate purposes. Broad language is common, but a highly specific use can reveal management priorities. Readers should also distinguish between primary shares, which raise money for the company, and secondary shares, which allow existing holders to sell part of their stake. Compare Claims Across Sections One of the best ways to read a prospectus is to compare the same idea in multiple places. If management emphasizes rapid customer adoption, check whether customer concentration is rising or falling. If efficiency is a major theme, examine whether operating expenses are growing more slowly than revenue. If the company describes a large addressable market, consider how much of that opportunity is realistically reachable with its current products. Cross-checking reduces the risk of evaluating isolated claims without context. Use a Reading Checklist A simple checklist can keep the review process focused. Start by writing down the company's main revenue sources, largest disclosed dependencies, recent growth rate, cash position, major expense categories, and expected use of IPO proceeds. Then note any unusual governance provisions, related-party transactions, or legal matters. Finally, identify the few assumptions that would most change the investment case if they proved wrong. This approach turns a long filing into a repeatable research process and makes later quarterly updates easier to compare with what the company originally disclosed. Conclusion A prospectus is most useful when treated as a structured set of questions rather than a document to read from page one to the end. Understand the business first, then examine risks, financial statements, ownership, dilution, and use of proceeds. The goal is not to predict the first day of trading. It is to understand what kind of company is entering the public market, what assumptions its story depends on, and which disclosures deserve continued attention after the listing.

articles.title: Sports Betting Promotion
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In July 2026, two major prediction exchanges recorded $53 billion in combined trading volume. Just two months earlier, that figure had stood at $26 billion. Pew Research Center analyst Kaitlyn Radde found that sports contracts accounted for most of the increase . The figures measure global trading activity rather than American gambling revenue, but they reveal how quickly a new form of sports-related speculation has developed. Traditional sportsbooks now compete for attention with businesses operating under federal financial regulations. To a customer watching an NFL game, the products can appear similar. The differences become important when an advertisement promises a bonus or encourages someone to open an account. The question facing regulators concerns how those offers should explain their financial terms. The Same Sporting Event Can Support Different Products Sportsbooks have long attracted customers through promotional credits and welcome offers. Covers reviews these services alongside legal online casinos, allowing readers to compare account conditions and available rewards. Its current promo details for FanDuel describe a November offer worth up to $200 in bonus bets. Eligible new customers must deposit at least $5 and place a qualifying $5 cash wager on four consecutive days. Each qualifying day earns a $50 bonus bet. The credits expire seven days after receipt and cannot be withdrawn as cash. The promotion requires no code and is scheduled to expire on November 22. Those conditions explain why the advertised maximum differs from the immediate financial value received by a customer. Prediction exchanges offer another arrangement. Customers purchase contracts connected to events, with prices reflecting the offers available from other participants. A contract trading at 60 cents may pay $1 if the predicted outcome occurs. The customer could earn 40 cents before fees, although a contrary result would leave the contract worthless. Such platforms can provide incentives for new accounts, but the governing arrangements differ from conventional sportsbook promotions. Customers need to examine trading fees and settlement conditions before comparing their financial value with familiar betting credits. Rapid Growth Has Intensified Competition for Attention Pew's September analysis found that sports contracts generated more trading volume than any other prediction category. During June and July, one exchange recorded over $58 billion in sports-related activity. Another approached $22 billion. The researchers counted contracts according to their full $1 settlement value rather than the actual amount customers paid. This distinction prevents the figures from serving as direct comparisons with traditional sportsbook spending. Nevertheless, they demonstrate the enormous volume of transactions taking place around sporting outcomes. America's established betting industry has experienced a different financial trend. The American Gaming Association reported that regulated sports wagering revenue fell 15.6% during August 2026 to $1 billion. Customers wagered $10.89 billion through traditional sportsbooks , representing a modest annual decline. The association identified prediction-market competition as one contributing factor, alongside changes to the sporting calendar. Its assessment reflects the position of an industry trade group rather than an independent determination of the cause. Still, the numbers illustrate why operators have a commercial interest in retaining customers as alternatives become more visible. Advertising Rules Have Become a Competitive Issue The American Gaming Association has examined the differences between the sectors' promotional activity. Its August research estimated that prediction businesses spent nearly $200 million on digital advertising during the first seven months of 2026. The organisation also reported that more than half of sports betting advertisements encountered by consumers came from operators outside state responsible-gaming requirements. Those figures belong to an industry-sponsored analysis, although they raise a significant policy question. Companies offering products connected to identical sporting outcomes may face different obligations concerning customer messaging. The distinction also concerns big tech platforms that determine where advertisements appear. In January 2026, Google amended its American advertising policy to permit promotions for prediction markets operated by qualifying federally regulated businesses. Advertisers must obtain certification and comply with the company's financial-services requirements. That policy provides access to digital advertising inventory without establishing that every promoted product qualifies as a state-licensed sportsbook. The arrangement illustrates how platform rules interact with federal authorisation, creating another consideration for customers trying to understand who supervises an advertised offer. State Regulators Have Their Own Consumer Standards New York's gambling advertising requirements provide an example of the existing state approach. Licensed sportsbooks must disclose material promotional terms and identify important limitations before customers participate. When an offer requires someone to wager money to obtain credits, advertisements must give the qualifying amount the same prominence as the reward. The state also prohibits promotions that describe transactions as free of risk when customers can lose their own funds. These rules establish expectations about how operators communicate financial commitments. The regulatory disagreement extends beyond advertising. In October, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday joined a bipartisan coalition supporting Supreme Court review of whether sports prediction contracts should follow state gambling laws. Federal regulators maintain authority over qualifying financial derivatives, while state officials argue that certain sports contracts function as gambling. The debate over the future of America includes the balance between national financial regulation and local consumer protection. Its outcome could influence the taxes companies pay and the account safeguards their customers receive. Public Confidence Deserves More Than Promotional Claims The expansion comes during a period of growing concern about sports integrity. Ipsos reported in October 2026 that 56% of Americans believed sports betting diminished the integrity of sporting competition. That represented an increase of 19 percentage points since 2023. The research also found that 68% of adults identified as fans of at least one sport. Those findings suggest that gambling companies address an audience with varied attitudes toward wagering. Many spectators want sporting information without feeling compelled to participate in a financial transaction. Independent research provides further context. Pew Research Center surveyed 9,916 American adults during 2025 and found that 43% considered widespread sports betting legalisation bad for society. That proportion had increased from 34% in 2022. Yet 22% reported placing a sports wager during the preceding year. The figures demonstrate that public concern and commercial participation can exist together. Customers may enjoy betting while supporting stronger consumer protections. Clear promotional terms offer one way for businesses to respond to those expectations.

articles.title: Improve Data Integrity
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Every report, invoice, and forecast a business produces is only as reliable as the data underneath it. When that data is wrong, the damage spreads quietly. Balances drift, orders lose their invoices, and teams start keeping their own spreadsheets because they no longer trust the system. For organizations running ASE, Sybase consulting experts help restore that trust by improving two things at once: the accuracy of stored data and the reliability of every transaction that changes it. Both sound technical, and in part they are. But the payoff is entirely practical. Finance closes the month without reconciliation headaches, customers see correct balances, and auditors find records that agree with each other. Two Goals That Depend on Each Other Data integrity and transaction consistency are closely related, yet they protect against different problems. The table below shows how they differ. Problems in one area often look like problems in the other, which is why tracing them takes experience. Many businesses bring in Sybase consulting experts once doubts about their data appear, because finding where an error started is usually harder than fixing it. How Consultants Improve Data Integrity 1. Measuring the Current State The work starts with facts rather than assumptions. Consultants run health checks on the database, look for duplicate and orphaned records, and compare key totals between ASE and the systems that rely on it. The result is a clear list of problems ranked by business impact, so effort goes where it matters most. This step often reveals that a handful of tables cause most of the trouble. A single customer table with duplicate entries, for example, can ripple into billing, reporting, and support systems at once. Fixing that one source usually does more good than chasing hundreds of individual errors downstream. 2. Building Business Rules Into the Database In many older systems, the rules that keep data clean live only inside application code. That works until a second application, a bulk import, or a quick script writes to the same tables without those checks. Consultants move the essential rules into the database itself. Keys stop duplicates, relationships between tables prevent orphaned records, and value checks keep entries within sensible limits. Once the database enforces these rules, every program has to follow them. 3. Cleaning Existing Data Safely New rules can't be switched on while bad data is still sitting in the tables. Consultants work with business owners to agree how each type of error should be corrected, then clean the data in small, controlled batches. This avoids disrupting daily operations and leaves a clear record of what changed. 4. Catching Damage Before It Spreads Storage problems can sit unnoticed for months while the server keeps running normally. Consultants set up regular integrity checks using ASE's built-in dbcc tools and make sure someone reviews the results. Catching a damaged page early turns a potential crisis into routine maintenance. How Consultants Improve Transaction Consistency 1. Making Every Change All or Nothing A transaction should either complete fully or leave no trace. In ASE, though, many errors stop only the current statement and let the rest of the transaction continue. Unless the code checks for that, part of the work can be saved while the rest is lost. Consultants review stored procedures and application code so every failure triggers a proper rollback. This one improvement often removes a whole category of puzzling partial updates. 2. Bringing Clarity to Transaction Settings ASE can start and end transactions in two different ways, and code written for one approach may behave unexpectedly under the other. Consultants document which approach each application uses and test against it. They also help teams choose how strictly transactions are isolated from one another, balancing accuracy against speed. 3. Keeping Copies of the Data in Sync Many ASE environments copy data to standby or reporting servers. Over time, those copies can drift because of one-sided manual fixes or errors during replication. Consultants compare the copies with the original on a regular schedule and correct whatever caused the gap, so every system reports the same numbers. 4. Making Recovery Accurate A backup restores whatever it captured, good or bad. Consultants make sure backups form an unbroken chain and that the database can be restored to a precise moment. That matters most when a faulty batch job needs to be undone, since the business can roll back to just before it ran instead of losing a full day of work. What Businesses Gain The improvements add up to something simple: data people can rely on. Finance teams spend less time reconciling figures, support teams stop running manual correction scripts, and audits go faster because records agree across systems. Just as important, a clean and well-documented database is far easier to upgrade or migrate later, including a move to SQL Server. There's a quieter benefit too. When people trust the system, they stop building workarounds around it. The side spreadsheets, manual checks, and duplicate reports that grew up to compensate for unreliable data can finally be retired, which saves time across every team that touches the numbers. Frequently Asked Questions What's the difference between data integrity and transaction consistency? Integrity is about whether stored data is correct and undamaged. Consistency is about whether each transaction leaves the database in a valid state. A business needs both to trust its numbers. Will adding database rules slow down applications? There's a small overhead when data is inserted or updated, but it's usually minor compared with the cost of cleaning up bad data later. Good indexing keeps the impact low. Can a faulty batch job be undone in ASE? Yes, if transaction log backups are complete. The database can be restored and rolled forward to just before the job ran, which is why an unbroken backup chain matters so much. Final Perspective Reliable data doesn't come from a single fix. It comes from rules the database enforces, storage that's checked regularly, transactions that complete fully or not at all, and recovery plans that have been tested. Sybase consulting experts strengthen each of these areas, so the figures a business depends on are figures it can trust. For organizations reviewing their own environment, the team at ralantech.com covers ASE consulting, ongoing administration, and SQL Server migration, which can help put a data quality review in context. A practical first step is an integrity assessment of your most important databases, since its findings show exactly where improvement should begin.

articles.title: Out-of-State Accident
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. After an accident away from home, you may be dealing with an unfamiliar insurer, medical bills from another state, and questions about where to find a lawyer. The nearest office may not be the right place to start. Focus your search on these checks: Check authorization. Verify the attorney's licensing and ask how they would be authorized to handle your case. Test relevant experience. Use the first conversation to learn how the lawyer handles cases like yours. Understand the agreement. Get fee and expense terms in writing before you sign. This guide provides general information, not advice about your case. An appropriately authorized attorney can review your circumstances. Find Someone Who Can Handle the Case Where It Belongs If you were injured in another state, ask where your claim could be brought, which rules apply, and who may represent you there. Your home address alone won't answer those questions. Start with the location of the accident. Ask whether the claim could be brought in that state and what other locations might be available. For example, Michigan Legal Center's October 2026 explanation says whether a particular Michigan court can hear a case depends on the claim and the defendant's connections to Michigan. That example illustrates why a lawyer needs to review more than where you live. For an accident in New Jersey, an NJ injury lawyer such as Garces, Grabler & LeBrocq is an option to research. Confirm who would handle the matter and whether that attorney is authorized to appear in the relevant court. The firm lists motor vehicle accidents, truck accidents, and workers' compensation among its practice areas. Ask which type of claim fits your circumstances. Check the individual attorney. An office address alone doesn't establish whether the lawyer handling your file can appear in the relevant court. Look the individual up in that state's official directory. Maryland's attorney listing treats active status as good standing and authorization to practice, and the State Bar of Texas shows any public disciplinary history on each attorney's online profile. Licensing status doesn't establish experience with your type of claim. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes participate by working with a locally admitted lawyer who actively participates. The ABA model rules describe a conditional route for temporary legal services, but current state rules control. Ask how the proposed arrangement would work and whether separate court approval is needed. Request a deadline review early. Maryland has a default three-year filing period for civil actions at law, subject to other Code provisions. That rule does not establish the deadline for an out-of-state accident. Ask an attorney to identify when your filing period begins and which deadlines apply. Use the First Conversation to Test the Fit Use the consultation to learn how the lawyer would approach your claim and whether their working style suits your needs. Bring questions and take notes so you can compare the answers afterward. Bring a useful file. Gather a short timeline, photographs, witness names and contact details, the report number, insurance correspondence, and whatever medical and wage records you have so far. If you exchanged insurance details with the other driver at the scene, include those as well. Ask about cases like yours. Ask how often the attorney handles your type of accident, how they approach disputed responsibility, and what evidence they would gather. Ask what information they need before discussing a possible recovery. If your injuries are severe, ask about experience with long-term care needs. For serious injuries in Texas, Stogner Trial Law describes its catastrophic-injury category as life-altering injuries requiring extensive medical care and long-term support. Notice how answers are given. Ask who will handle the matter, how updates work, and what you can do from home rather than in person. Texas Court Help notes that one of a lawyer's most important duties is keeping the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter. Follow up by asking whom to contact with questions and how to send new records. Write down the proposed communication arrangements. Know What You Are Agreeing To Under a contingency-fee arrangement, the attorney's fee depends on a recovery. Expenses may be handled separately, so review both in the written agreement. Separate fees from expenses. The attorney's fee is one item; litigation expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, are another. Ask whether medical liens, or claims for repayment of medical costs, could also reduce what you receive. Review any firm's written agreement for the percentage and expense terms that would apply to your case. Texas Disciplinary Rule 1.04(d) requires contingent-fee agreements to be in writing and to state whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated. The order affects your share. Ask which method applies, what the percentage is, and whether it changes if the case goes to trial. Confirm the scope. Ask who is responsible for the case, whether another firm or local counsel may participate, and what work is included. If you are considering a firm for a serious injury claim, ask it to explain how its contingency arrangement applies to your matter, what case expenses you may owe, and who would handle the work. Use the same questions with every firm you compare. Read before signing. The ABA model fee rule calls for a written contingent-fee agreement signed by the client, though current state rules govern. Ask for explanations of any terms you don't understand, including what expenses, if any, you could owe without a recovery. Get the agreement in writing and keep a copy for your records. The same care applies later in the claim. Accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that bars future claims tied to the accident, so take your time with any offer and keep your statements to insurers calm and factual before agreeing to a number. Conclusion The right lawyer after an out-of-state accident is the one who can work where your claim belongs, has handled cases like yours, and explains the agreement clearly. Start by confirming that the attorney is authorized in the state where your case would be heard, then use the consultation to compare how each lawyer would approach your claim and keep you informed. Before you sign, make sure the fee percentage, the expense terms, and the people handling your file are all set out in writing. Taking those steps early protects your filing deadline and puts you in a stronger position for the rest of the claim. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a lawyer licensed in the state where the accident happened? Usually, the attorney who appears in court on your claim needs to be authorized in that state. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes take part by working with a locally admitted lawyer, but each state's rules decide when that is allowed. Ask any firm you speak with how it would be authorized to handle your case. How do personal injury lawyers charge for their work? Many work on a contingency basis, which means the fee depends on a recovery. Case expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, may be handled separately. The written agreement should explain the percentage, how expenses are treated, and what you could owe if there is no recovery. What should I bring to a first consultation? Bring a short timeline of the accident, photographs, witness contact details, the police report number, insurance correspondence, and any medical and wage records you have. A complete file helps the lawyer assess your claim and gives you a fair basis for comparing firms. How long do I have to file a personal injury claim? Filing deadlines vary by state and by type of claim. Maryland's default period for civil actions at law is three years, and Texas generally allows two years from the date of injury for personal injury lawsuits. Because other rules can change the deadline, ask an attorney to confirm when your filing period begins. Should I accept the insurance company's first settlement offer? Take time to review any offer before agreeing to it. A settlement usually comes with a release that ends future claims tied to the accident, even if your injuries later turn out to be more serious. Make sure you understand the full extent of your losses before you sign.

articles.title: Field Notes From the Spanish General Strike
articles.author: Kit Wainer
articles.content: The November 11 Spanish general strike was the product of social movement protests around the cost of living that have been bubbling for at least two years. Housing rights struggles have sprung up around the country, as rising real estate values combined with low salaries have made rents nearly unaffordable for much of the working class. Housing unions began discussing calls for a general strike at least a year ago. It was the September 23 eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at age 87 that sparked outrage throughout the country. Her death less than two weeks later galvanized calls for the general strike. Most of the union federations got on board after the movement agreed to demand both lower rents and higher salaries. In Catalunya organizing for the strike was led by the “Ens Costa La Vida” (it costs us our lives) coalition, based on an alliance between housing rights organizations and the smaller union federations. For weeks in advance coalition committees flyered and postered and did outreach in workplaces and schools. Estimates are that 4 million people participated in the general strike. The extent to which workers shut down their workplaces varied from region to region. The movement continues today with protests for housing rights and for freedom for those arrested during the general strike. In an effort to synchronize with the French protests which now take place every Saturday, the teachers unions in Catalunya organized a protest march for school funding and teacher salaries on November 21. The hope now is that workers learned the lessons of how to organize co-workers, and that the housing activists will see how popular their demands are and will continue the struggle. October 12: A Month to Prepare The Sant Marti banner reads, in Catalan, “We’ll stop the housing business.” This is a play off a central slogan of the housing rights movement: “Housing is a right, not a business.” I attended my neighborhood meeting for planning the general strike in the Spanish state on November 11. I live in Barcelona and went to the meeting for the Sant Martí barri (neighborhood). The planning meeting was attended by a little over 100 people. Sant Martí is a long group of smaller neighborhoods that runs east-west, north of the center of the city. It includes Poblenou, once an industrial center and now a rapidly gentrifying and increasingly expensive area with a boulevard that runs right up to the sea. Further west (away from the sea and toward the mountains) are groups of very working-class and sometimes impoverished areas. West of that, where I live, is El Clot, a working- and middle-class area that is very Catalan, a bit less expensive than Poblenou. The meeting was conducted in Catalan, as are nearly all left or movement meetings here. The actions in Catalunya are being organized by the “Ens Costa La Vida” coalition, an alliance of housing rights unions and minority labor unions (such as the General Confederation of Labour, or CGT). The meeting lasted about 90 minutes and the attendees were mostly young. The four chairs were young people (under 35), three of whom were women. After briefly presenting the reasons for the strike planned for November 11, they opened the meeting up to discussion. The general strike has the backing of several union federations who are part of the larger coalition involved in planning, but it was mostly the tenants’ unions that organized this neighborhood meeting. An Anticapitalistes comrade made some practical suggestions about getting the word out, and then we broke up into four committees: workplace outreach, education institutions, social movement alliances, and agitation/propaganda. I joined the last one. Mostly, we just quickly reviewed how we can get flyers out and where we can carry banners. We meet again as a subcommittee next Monday; a WhatsApp group was set up for the 30 or so of us on the committee. There are at least four or five other neighborhood meetings like this taking place around the city. Now neighborhood groups use a template to advertise strike preparation meetings. November 11: The Strike Anticapitalistes contingent preparing to march in the morning. 10:00 AM. I arrive at the Glòries shopping mall. This is part of the international Westfield chain which has several malls in the United States as well. We block off the entrance to the mall. A CGT contingent had gone inside to make sure everything was shut. Another CGT contingent marches to another location. Many youth from the housing rights unions were standing in front of the entrance. When the organizers realize we have more than enough to block the gates, they ask us to spread down the block to block off McDonald’s. That results in that store closing down as well. Messages keep circulating on our WhatsApp list. Urgent requests for people to come help block other neighborhood locations. Small groups respond. A message on the Anticapitalistes Telegram channel says that the construction work on the Rambla (the main tourist attraction) has been shut. I see in front of me the major street construction sites along Avinguda Diagonal are also empty. These are both massive and long-lasting infrastructure projects. Banners blocking Glòries. Left, “Raise salaries, dignified housing, strike committee.” Right: “No more evictions. Expropriate the vulture funds.” 10:15 AM. Suddenly the crowd outside the Glòries gate is swelled by district strike committee members emerging from inside the mall reporting that everything is shut. We have far more people than we need and contingents begin to form to shut down other places. 10:30 AM. I follow a contingent of maybe 75 people toward the Poblenou neighborhood. They are chanting, “People without houses, houses without people, can’t understand.” (It rhymes and sounds better in Catalan). The UGT banner telling construction workers not to work here. 10:45 AM. The contingent now seems to have at least 100, with many CGT banners. Some messages circulate on our district WhatsApp group acknowledging the difficulty of coordinating so many contingents. 11:00 AM. On Rambla del Poblenou, a major tourist and commercial boulevard, we stop to block the Four Points Sheraton Hotel. Hotels and shopping malls are targeted because of their roles in bidding up real estate prices. A few dozen move into the lobby to chant strike slogans. “Long live the struggle of the working class!” Eventually we are kicked out. Actually, shutting this down was never plausible given all the guests inside. Closing down a convenience store. 11:15 AM. We march further along the Rambla del Poblenou to temporarily block PrimaPrix, a chain store. Our people have filled the entrance of Mercadona, a major supermarket chain. Customers can exit but newer shoppers are turned away. The store sets off the fire alarm, which draws no response from the police parked a block away. Finally, management agrees to shut the metal curtain and the window shades. The protesters emerge cheering. An additional chant now, “A-Anti-Anticapitalistes!” After marching around to find other targets to shut, we return to Mercadona and see it is still shut. At that point two groups of elementary school students, led by their teachers, march up Poblenou. They stop by us and we all exchange exuberant cheers. Teachers and students have played a major role in the buildup to this day. Every school in our neighborhood has been adorned with protest and general strike signs, complaining of underfunding, lack of housing for the students, and lack of support services. Closing a major supermarket. The sign reads: “Students and teachers on strike.” Dozens had filled the entrance chanting strike slogans, ultimately forcing the store to close. Turning the corner we shut down another supermarket, Bonpreu. A report was posted on the Anticapitalistes list that 50-65% of commerce had closed in Barcelona. My thoroughly subjective glance around the neighborhood is consistent with that. There are some bars and small restaurants open, especially those that belong to larger café chains. But at least half have their shutters down. For the establishments the protesters closed, the result was more disruption than full closure, as many seemed able to reopen later in the day. The intent was also to reach workers inside. There were few conflicts with employees in these stores. The one exception was at Bonpreu, where one protester appeared to have expropriated an apple. 5:00 PM. The main march. Feeder groups converge on Passeig de Gràcia, a major commercial and tourist boulevard which reminds me of New York’s 5th Avenue, but in Catalan modernisme style. The photos and captions tell the story. The crowd has been estimated at 400,000. I’ve seen reports of mass rallies in the Basque Country, Valencia, and Madrid so far. In Madrid there were 500,000 in the streets, and that number might have been higher had it not rained so hard there. (Fortunately, the rains came to Barcelona only later in the evening.) The crowd was so massive, packed, and slow-moving it was hard to see all the contingents there. But the energy levels were quite high. The Anticapitalistes led those around us in singing one of the songs from the French protests, translated into Catalan. A group of French students, who had come to support the general strike, joined in and then sang the original French version. The rally was larger than many of the organizers seemed to expect, which is good given the deep crisis into which the Spanish state is about to enter. Most expect a center-right government to emerge from the snap elections called for on November 29. In my district committee, the very young leaders had said all along that the general strike was the best way to prepare for the fight against a right-wing government. [This article adapts two pieces that first appeared in Against the Current : “ A Month to Prepare for the General Strike ” and “ Notes on the General strike in Barcelona, 11 November 2026 .”] The post Field Notes From the Spanish General Strike appeared first on The Call .
