articles.title: Mass Deportation Disaster
articles.author: Joe Mathews
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty. It will need two amnesties. One for the millions of victims of the cruel, violent, and flagrantly unlawful deportation campaign tearing through American communities. And another for those who took part in making the deportations happen. The Trump administration is deporting people without due process, including to faraway continents and unfamiliar countries. Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway. Families have been shattered, human rights cancelled, local economies damaged, and whole segments of society forced into hiding. Related: How the University of California Became Both a Gateway and a Gatekeeper When this nightmare finally ends, California and the United States will face a monumental challenge: How do we reunite families, uncover the full scale of what was done in our name, compensate victims, restore the rule of law, and hold official perpetrators accountable? The solution is what I am calling the Double Amnesty. The first amnesty is straightforward: a comprehensive, unencumbered program granting permanent residency, and creating a speedy process for obtaining citizenship for everyone caught in the U.S. regime’s anti-immigrant pogrom. This first amnesty starts with allowing readmission for deported people, with priority going to immigrants the Trump administration sent to third-party countries. Restitution must apply universally—to undocumented immigrants, long-term legal residents, migrants with temporary status, and U.S. citizens mistaken for migrants. The amnesty must also cover citizens and residents who were punished or injured for defending their neighbors against deportation. They are heroes, not criminals. This is the only practical way to return millions of human beings to the light, stabilize our economy, and shrink the unauthorized population. The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members. It also reduced unauthorized immigration to the country . Immigration restrictionists claim that relentless enforcement deters unauthorized presence. In reality, the opposite is true . When people are arrested in immigration courts or naturalization appointments, the message is: Stay undocumented, stay in the shadows. The current administration has manufactured more undocumented immigration, not reduced it. By stripping legal status en masse — revoking Temporary Protected Status (TPS) , ending protection for Dreamers , rescinding humanitarian parole , and ripping away valid visas —the government deliberately and illegally created more than 1 million so-called “illegal” immigrants. Related: California’s Climate Law Still Matters Globally Which brings me to the second amnesty of the Double Amnesty—in which the U.S. would offer administrative and legal relief to the government employees, ICE agents, CBP officers, and bureaucrats who participated in executing this campaign. This amnesty may be harder to swallow. Many of us would prefer to prosecute law enforcement officials who broke the law and hurt immigrants, but the scale of the lawless deportation campaign makes mass prosecutions impractical. But the second amnesty does not offer forgiveness automatically. This amnesty must be strictly contingent on first establishing personal and institutional accountability, and on exposing violations. The Trump deportation machine operates in the dark, with masked law enforcement personnel, secret deportations to third countries, concealed detainee facilities, and undisclosed transfers of migrants between centers and prisons to keep them from being found by families and lawyers. As a result, deportations have been executed with staggering incompetence, shielded by bureaucratic deception, and deliberately hidden from federal courts, defense lawyers, and the public . We still do not know the true number of missing children, falsified records, or unconstitutional orders carried out in field offices across the country. To earn this second amnesty, agents and officials must go through a process of mandatory truth-telling. They must step forward and disclose every secret directive and unwritten quota, every illegal detention and unconstitutional maneuver, and every document or record withheld from courts, defense counsel, and the public. Related: Dear America: You Don't Really Know Gavin Newsom In addition, the top executives of private companies that knew of the immigration abuses and personally profited must report their activities—and forfeit every dollar they made, for their business and personally—to a restitution fund for the campaign’s victims. Once perpetrators provide full, verifiable documentation of their actions, they should receive immunity. If they lie, destroy evidence, or refuse to disclose, they must face full criminal prosecution. There is one non-negotiable exception to the amnesty: No mercy at the top. Zocalo Market Square

articles.title: War on Migrants
articles.author: Kate Morrissey
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Human rights monitors from across the Americas met twice in Mexico earlier this year to hold a people’s tribunal over aggressive actions committed by the United States under the Trump administration. On Thursday, the jury from that tribunal announced its preliminary findings during a press conference in Mexico City, with some participants joining virtually from as far away as Brazil. Based on testimony and evidence from more than 50 cases heard over four days, ranging from military attacks on fishing boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean to deportations of immigrants to countries where they do not have ties , the group roundly condemned the United States’ human rights violations and called on international organizations — including the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights — to launch investigations. “There’s an overwhelming number of cases and issues that are presented there, but from the most local to the more global geopolitical issues that are at stake, we see this common thread of breaking with the rule of law in an advanced stage of capitalism that requires, for its own survival, intensification of looting and land grabs and violation of rights and extermination and even ecocide and genocide of certain populations,” said Laura Carlsen, director of MIRA: Feminisms and Democracies, in a call with Capital & Main. The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main. “All illegal aliens receive full due process and have their claims heard,” said Lauren Bis, a spokesperson for the White House. “No lawbreakers in the history of human civilization have been treated better than illegal aliens.” The tribunal, co-founded about 16 years ago by roughly a half-dozen people from several countries and known as Tribunal Internacional de Conciencia de los Pueblos en Movimiento, or International Tribunal of Conscience of Peoples in Movement , met in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico, in September and in Mexico City in October after a series of pre-hearings in several countries including Colombia and the U.S. Camilo Pérez-Bustillo, co-founder of Witness at the Border and of the tribunal, explained that the people’s tribunal traces back to a tribunal organized in 1967 by acclaimed philosophers and writers Bertrand Russell and Jean-Paul Sartre to examine war crimes committed during the Vietnam War. That tribunal took its inspiration from the Nuremberg Trials that prosecuted Nazi officials after World War II, Pérez-Bustillo said. A similar, international tribunal has operated in Italy since the late 1970s. Related: Los Angeles Leads the Nation in Reported ICE Enforcement Incidents “The first commitment of the tribunal is to center the victim in the process,” José Antonio Foronda Farro, an attorney who is leading the jury’s legal review process and co-founded the tribunal, said in Spanish during Thursday’s press conference. Foronda Farro, who specializes in human rights, migration and environmental law, said one of the tribunal’s goals is to be able to denounce the human rights violations it has documented before international organizations, including the United Nations and international courts that hear human rights cases. He said the people’s tribunal itself doesn’t have any sentencing power over the government officials that it is judging, but he still sees the practice as worthwhile. “It’s good to make it visible,” Foronda Farro said in an interview with Capital & Main. “It’s good to spread it.” He said he sees the people’s tribunal as a process rather than an event and emphasized that even the conclusions that the group will share in December won’t be truly final because of the ongoing witnessing, documenting and listening the group will be doing. Carlsen, who participated on the jury, said beyond examining rights violations and broken laws, the tribunal is also looking at what it sees as the impunity that the U.S. government and its officials operate with. “We have seen this leading to a level of dispossession, disappearance, discrimination and displacement, among many other crimes — many against humanity — and that we have not seen in other moments in history,” Carlsen said in Spanish during the press conference. Julio Moreira, professor of sociology and law at Universidade Federal da Integração Latino-Americana in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil, said he was particularly concerned about the U.S. government’s attempts to meddle in other countries’ elections, including in Brazil and Honduras. “We are connected to political issues in a way that isn’t tied to any specific partisan politics,” Moreira said in Spanish. “Rather, it is a politics of humanity.” Related: He Won Protection From Torture: Then ICE Deported Him to Mexico The jury will release a final report in December that will include a specific review of individual international laws and conventions it said was broken by the U.S. government. In the meantime, the preliminary findings provide a resounding indictment of the Trump administration’s policies and practices. The jury organized its findings around four themes — genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity; neofascism and U.S. intervention; migrant genocide and carceral imperialism; and environmental justice and ecocide. “In the United States, migrant people are assassinated and persecuted, creating a regime of terror that reaches even U.S. citizens who dare to intervene in the arbitrary detention of migrants,” the report says. In addition, the jury writes in the report that the U.S. also promotes similar policies in other countries, such as Mexico’s use of its National Guard to block migrants heading north. It says that throughout the hemisphere, migrants are treated as criminals, and their rights are taken away — even their right to life. According to the report, the testimony and evidence that the jury received regarding migration practices included information about unaccompanied migrant children, Indigenous migrants, forced displacement, mass deportation, Haitians stuck at the border in Tijuana, migrants living in a camp in Mexico City and deportation flights to Brazil. The final report will include more specific details from the cases, Carlsen said. The report says that migrants experience different types of economic exploitation on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, noting that many immigration detention facilities are run by private companies. As of January 2025, nearly 90% of people in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody were in facilities run by private prisons, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse , which gathers and analyzes government data. The U.S. government often transfers people in immigration custody to detention centers far away from their families, friends and lawyers, making it more difficult for them to fight their cases, according to the report. “The United States expands the carceral system as a form of torture to dehumanize migrants,” the report says. It says that deportations occur without following a legal process and that the U.S. government doesn’t necessarily deport people to their countries of origin, but rather to other places. Related: Trump Deports Immigrants to Countries the U.S. Says Are Unsafe It calls out what it says is the racism, xenophobia and discrimination involved in these policies as detrimental to the mental and physical well-being of migrants by exposing them to violence, isolating them and breaking up family and other social ties. The report notes that many groups, including U.S. citizens creating networks to protect Latino migrants, cross-border legal defense networks, shelters and sanctuary cities, are resisting the Trump administration’s policies and trying to support migrants both in the U.S. and abroad. The report calls for protection of migrants’ rights to mobility and for the U.S. to stop considering migration a crime. It urges the U.S. to implement a right to refuge and asylum and guarantee migrants’ rights to health, food, education and work. It calls for an end to attacks, persecution and torture of migrants and human rights defenders as well as to arbitrary detentions and deportations. It says the U.S. should end third country agreements and close detention centers. The report calls on the U.S. to guarantee the return of essential documents to migrants, which, the jury learned during testimony, often does not happen. And, the report says the U.S. should guarantee the right to truth, justice and reparations for the victims of the country’s harmful policies. Elena Gutiérrez, from Movimiento de los Pueblos por la Paz con Justicia, or Movement of the Peoples for Peace and Justice , and Global Exchange called on people in the U.S., Mexico, Canada and the whole of Latin America to organize across borders to defend human rights. The group will present its final report in different locations throughout December, beginning in Mexico City on Dec. 9, the anniversary of the U.N. adopting the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide , and ending in New York in front of the United Nations on Dec. 18, International Migrants Day . Related: She Came to America Seeking Refuge. Now She Fears for Her Life in ICE Detention In a call with Witness at the Border members earlier last week, Pérez-Bustillo pointed out that Dec. 10 is Human Rights Day . “It was the same body of human beings who were thinking about the same issues, who had sort of the same questions in mind that adopted the Genocide Convention one day, and the next day adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, so we want to think about those two instruments and what they represent and sort of the thinking that went into them in a convergent way,” Pérez-Bustillo said. “And that’s the grounding from which the tribunal emerges.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Melat Kiros
articles.author: Ann Garrison
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On November 11th, Colorado’s First-District Congresswoman-elect Melat Kiros, who represents Denver, joined seven other newly elected members in voting against uber Zionist and corporatist Hakeem Jeffries to lead the Democratic Party in the House. Just two days later, the Denverite published “ Melat Kiros may face a notable Democratic challenger in 2028 ,” an announcement that establishment Democrat Crisanta Duran had formed an exploratory committee to consider a run against Kiros back in September, two months before voters had even gone to the polls. The emerging Democratic Party’s civil war will soon be in full force and getting uglier than it already has. The Clinton-Obama moderates, who aren't really moderate at all, are already trying to take back what they lost to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), including Melat Kiros and five more Congressional electeds on November 3. Another anti-war, anti-Zionist advocate for Medicare-for-All, Ohio’s Don Leonard, also says he wants a Constitutional Amendment to overturn Citizens United, the Supreme Court decision that opened the floodgates to special interest money controlling US elections. The “moderates” who have hold of the levers of power no doubt hate these young new, non-white DSA members of Congress even more than they despise MAGA. Why? Because, for one, should they stick to DSA’s espoused principles, they could make faux progressive members of Congress look bad, as they just did in the vote for Speaker. Related: Rwanda's Transnational Prosecutions and Narrative Grip Note, however, that they also made two of their own, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib, look bad. What kind of socialist or even progressive votes to so hugely empower a Black man who, in 2014, spoke to over 10,000 people at a “New York Stands with Israel” rally during Israel’s Operation Protective Edge massacres in Gaza. A Black man who kept chanting variations of, “Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel Forever!”, echoing the late Alabama Governor George Wallace’s rallying cry, “Segregation today, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever!” Who said that Israel lived in a tough neighborhood where it should not apologize for its strength, then joined in the next ten years of hostilities that led to the US-Israeli War on Iran, while taking more than $1.7 million in AIPAC donations and affirming his devotion at the Wailing Wall in Jerusalem? The incoming DSA electeds exposed those two already there, along with all the other faux progressives who have no red lines, not even genocide. And how did DSA respond? As soon as the votes were counted, New York DSA held a national Zoom to draft AOC for president. Even on the outside, they would seem to have no red lines either. In 2024, AOC joined fellow progressives in, they said, opposing offensive weapons to Israel while supporting defensive systems like Iron Dome, and voted against Marjorie Taylor Greene's amendment to cut $500 million from the system because it left offensive aid untouched. In 2026, she made a big splash at a DSA conference by saying she now opposes all military aid to Israel because they can afford to pay for it themselves. (With US aid, or given that US taxpayers pick up so many of their bills for things like universal health insurance?) The Democratic Party slugfest is on despite the compliance of DSA’s biggest star and most likely presidential candidate with the Zionist agenda. Related: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize and the Dark Legacy of the Rwanda Tribunal Democratic strategist James Carville, Bill Clinton’s 1992 campaign manager, was named Campaign Manager of the Year by the American Association of Political Consultants after helping Clinton beat George Herbert Walker Bush, but in October 2026, he said he would rather Republicans keep a five-seat House majority than have Democrats win by five seats and be "hostage to the DSA." He clearly treats them as a greater threat to his party than MAGA. The Democrats predictably won by closer to 40 seats, so it must have been those five DSA seats that Carville saw coming. Perhaps he fears that in a close vote with a lot of “moderates” voting with MAGA, the DSA voters could be a small but significant block. Establishment Democrats saw his coming Denver is a Democratic town, so Kiros won her seat back in June, when she upset Diane DeGette, a 15-term incumbent who had held onto the seat for 30 years. Kiros had never held political office though she did belong to the Denver chapter of DSA, and she had soared to prominence when she sacrificed her job by refusing to un-publish “ Dear US Law Firms ,” a Medium editorial responding to an open letter published by 100 major U.S. law firms (including her then-employer, Sidley Austin, LLP). The lawyers had urged law schools to take a strong stance against anti-Semitism and Islamophobia on campus and specifically treated “calls for the elimination of the Israeli state” as a form of anti-Semitism. Kiros responded that they were conflating criticism with anti-Semitism, that Israel had weaponized charges of anti-Semitism to defend apartheid, ethnic cleansing, and collective punishment against Palestinians. She cited human rights groups accusing Israel of apartheid and framed the conflict’s roots in the Balfour Declaration and British colonialism, the 1948 Nakba (which she pointed out involved mass killings and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians), and ongoing restrictions on Palestinians. She also referenced statements by some Israeli officials that she viewed as genocidal in rhetoric regarding Gaza. She argued for a one-state solution with equal rights for all. That is quite a contrast to AOC, who went into Congress saying that she was no expert on Israel and Palestine. DSA Denver responded with an extraordinary organizing effort that drew in volunteers from around the country. Kiros upset DeGette, who outspent her by roughly $2 million overall, with much of the money pouring in near the end of the race when it was clear Kiros had taken the lead. Related: Ethiopia vs. Eritrea: A New War Could Send Oil and Gas Prices Soaring Similar contests are likely to shape up in the next two years, with DSA trying to out-organize and fundraise establishment Dems with corporate and oligarch money to burn. How many more millions would they be willing to spend to see whether someone as bland as Cristana Duran can take on Melat Kiros? Like AOC, Kiros is likely here to stay, but how will she and the others who dared say no to Jeffries vote in another two years? After their votes against Jeffries, they would probably be assigned to Dogcatching and Garbage Pickup Committees if they existed. There will no doubt be charges of anti-Semitism at every turn. They’re not likely to be given much to take home to their constituents in the way of jobs and civic improvements. DSA has changed the political landscape, and more battles are looming, but AOC’s rising star doesn’t promise radical change. It nevertheless seems only fair to let the six who voted no to “Israel today, tomorrow, and forever” take their seats and see what they can do. Black Agenda Report

articles.title: Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
articles.author: Henry Snow
articles.content: At a conference in Orlando, Florida, in 2005, the American billionaire Charles Koch gave a speech explaining how he and his audience could protect “freedom and prosperity in the world.” While accepting an award named after potato chip magnate Herman Lay, Koch explained that he had conceived a “science of liberty,” which he described as “the study and practice of sustainably advancing liberty to create prosperity and social progress.” The solution lay, Koch said, in economic analysis — treating every interaction between people as a market exchange. He claimed this “Market Process Analysis” helped him build not only his fortune but also his family life and interpersonal interactions. Out of it, he created what he called Market-Based Management (MBM), a theory for managing workers and his business. The science of liberty he outlined in Orlando applied those same principles to government — in America and around the world. Playing God Workers at Charles Koch’s web of companies felt differently. One anonymous Koch employee in Wichita wrote that their colleagues were “walking around like they are in the George Orwell book, ‘ 1984 ,’” terrified of the Koch family, the “only major employer in the area,” who used their power “to control the employees and their movement within the other Koch entities.” Another, in Atlanta, called Koch’s extensive training in MBM “brainwashing.” The atmosphere, others reported, was “cult-like,” and employees were “noticeably unhappy,” with fifty-hour workweeks as well as mandatory overtime and weekend work. A software engineer in Bangalore wrote that at Koch’s companies “managers are GOD. . . . They can play with anyone’s life.” Some of these disgruntled employees, hoping to convince management to change their ways, insisted they were not “practicing what they preached” — that MBM’s values were good and simply being misapplied. But Charles Koch had worked on the system for decades. He personally cultivated its materials, and his company forced employees to study them for upward of five hours a week, according to one review. Some of the values in Koch’s system of MBM were simply anodyne — “respect” is its ninth “guiding principle.” But the underlying purpose of the philosophy was to extract maximum profit from employees. Science of Control The science of liberty seemed more like a science of control. Koch’s “science” relied on four connected claims about human behavior that structure economic and political life across the globe today. First, that we should analyze society as merely a collection of individuals, an idea known as methodological individualism. Second, the claim that individuals are motivated only by self-interest, generally though not exclusively in the form of material incentives — or psychological egoism. Third, an insistence that deliberate planning cannot be trusted: humans are too selfish, and too limited, to make or execute grand plans for society. We should trust the competitive evolution of markets over the cooperative intention of democracy. And fourth, the belief that everything is — and should be — a market. The world consists of competing individuals, and social science exists to figure out how to structure that competition so prosperity arises out of it. This paradigm is known as market fundamentalism. Proponents of these ideas present them as inescapable truths about the world, like gravity. If we know how human beings will act, there is no need to speak of how they should act. Thus, “there is no alternative,” as the Victorian philosopher Herbert Spencer put it, to these cruel calculations: they are an inescapable truth about human action. Political Visions But these ideas are not scientific truths that experts have discovered. They are political visions that ideologues have created. There are other ways we can live and work, and generally most people prefer those alternatives when asked and frequently pursue them when we are not. From Samuel Bentham’s program of mechanized and precarious shipbuilding labor to Frederick Winslow Taylor’s floundering efforts to optimize pig iron loading, supposedly optimal methods for manipulating workers have generally failed — until their architects relied on political and economic force to impose their ideas anyway. Four hundred years of elite scheming have failed to produce either the technocratic control that utilitarians like the Benthams wanted or the pure competition advocated by market radicals like Ludwig von Mises. Every country in the world, even those with little or no political freedom, has major movements that demand better. Those movements do not always win. But every victory builds a foundation for the next. Today we have labor rights, voting power, and political freedoms — where we have them — because of the hard work of those who came before us. Building on their legacy, we can continue to make a better world now and to create conditions for yet more advances after we are gone. Control science is not “human nature.” It is not “how the world works.” It is not just orthodox economics or economic common sense or advanced political discourse. Identifying the different intertwining strands that give control science its strength and naming the total result, helps us take it on. Labeling control science — and labeling it accurately as a matter of control — is all the more important because of how it works. Rule Without Rulers The irony of control science is that it is ultimately not a theory of control by anyone at all. Control science respects no kings, no presidents, and no gods but what one of Herbert Spencer’s followers called “that awful One to whom it is profanity to pray.” This is an ideology for control by no one, of everyone. Its advocates call this freedom. The science of control is an attempt at rule without rulers, an abstract authoritarianism, an art of excuses: centuries of elites finding themselves in positions of power and scrambling to justify that power to themselves and the world. This vast program of institutionalized apathy has been developed through, and always relies on, the forceful control of workers themselves. Identifying this program does two things for us. First, it makes clear that cynical claims about “human nature” are social and political constructions, not an objective truth discovered by capitalists. Second, then, this intellectual history of economic thought reveals how much it has always been about control of us, not by us. We can rally against it accordingly: control science is fake, and it is wrong. Ideas alone will not be enough, of course. Control science has succeeded by embedding itself in the legal, political, and economic structures of the world around us. It does not describe actual human nature, but it does describe how many people do, and must, act, precisely because of the way capitalists have made the world. Selfishness is embedded in the real material relations we have with each other: the most responsible strategies for investing, for example, may include investments in oil companies. The cheapest products are produced under the worst labor conditions. Buying better or investing differently as an individual will accomplish little, and it is difficult to build collective movements around doing something that makes us, temporarily, worse off, in a world of economic scarcity and against constant competition by the preachers of selfishness. We cannot defeat control science as individual consumers. But we can as workers, as voters, and as full human beings. Over the last four centuries, many of the greatest victories for justice, equality, and freedom have relied on mass movements of working people, from the revolutions of the eighteenth century to the New Deal and decolonization in the twentieth century. Workers’ Control The twenty-first century has been, in much of the world, a period of defeat and retreat for working-class left-wing politics. But it does not have to be that way. The science of control was made in the workplace. It can be unmade there as well. Labor organizing forces idealistic progressives to ground our projects in material incentives: better wages, improved working conditions, more free time. This is particularly necessary in the cynical world control science has made. We have been told that everyone is selfish and that an alternative world is impossible. This makes it all the more difficult to believe rousing appeals to empathy and ethics alone. Organizing within workplaces must become part of a broader movement for democracy and equality at work — control by workers, not of them. Most of us recoil at the idea of an absolute monarch or a dictator. Yet we spend a good portion of our days, and our lives, doing the bidding of bosses over whom we have little power. We should abhor authoritarian company “presidents” and company boards the way we do dictatorship and monarchy. Working people should wield power through robust and assertive democratic unions to force our bosses to take our needs and desires and dreams into account. A powerful labor movement alone will not end the science of control. And an economy of competing democratic cooperatives would still be one driven by markets and competition. Thus, we also need to aim for democratic control of the economy writ large. Human needs and collective desires, not the movement of markets, should determine what we make and do. A market is a forever skewed democracy: your voting power is proportional to your wealth, and the most exploitative actors are therefore the most powerful. We should find this an offense against democracy, and we should act accordingly. Rule by market rules has only succeeded in leading us to a world that satisfies no one. Mass working-class movements, wielding the power of democracy, can build an intentional and deliberate world that reflects our most meaningful and deeply held collective wants, democratically aggregated, rather than our individual purchasing choices, scaled by our wealth. We can build our moral principles and our material needs into the legal structure, social fabric, and collective ideals of our societies so that acting in the common good, instead of against it, becomes easier and more obvious every day. A Collective Program We know collective effort can outcompete nihilist competition, because it has done so before: an imperfect fraction of this program of economic democracy saved the world from fascism. Imagine what a full-fledged collective program could do for living standards, economic growth, and climate change. Through public housing authorities, we can determine where housing is built and how much it costs based on our need for comfortable homes, instead of the political demand to keep housing prices up for those already locked into an expensive mortgage. With utility nationalization, we can replace hated telecommunications monopolies with less expensive, more functional infrastructure that we control. All of this requires no promises of or belief in a socialist utopia (though it will help us move toward one). Right now, it is right-wing economics that is in the way of lower rent, higher wages, shorter hours, full employment, and economic dignity, for all of us. If we take control of our work and our lives, we can secure a better life together. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat. . . . He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit. But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations — a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting. Amazon — a company known for fast delivery — had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day but no chair. She was moved to a different position but still required to lift heavy packages. Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at eighty hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation but stopped, because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says. The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up; Amazon fired her. Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave. Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance , a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all US workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon. Systematic Violations Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law, “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that. “Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.” Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.) Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant. Pattern of Illegality Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say yes, they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say no, Amazon puts them on unpaid leave , which rapidly runs out. Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700. . . . I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat. “Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.” Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.) Tragic Results Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly ten-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it. She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse. Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out . Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child. Law Reduces Miscarriages When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law. But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around fifty thousand workers. “When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.” Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said. “Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.” Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved. But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also s ued Amazon for this. Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws. Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond. Pace Drives Injuries The worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group. Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible — or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic .” In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination. California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it. Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal. Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal. Is There a Policy? Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from forty states responded, and eighty-one described loss of a pregnancy. (Get more info on Warehouse Life here .) Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mount Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon board of directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record. Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said. When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “ Delay. Deny. Discipline .” March on HR The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the five-thousand-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April. The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant. The union sent several workers to accompany her to HR, saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections. The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.” “It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: General strike in Greece rejects militarization and austerity
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: A nationwide general strike in Greece drew tens of thousands onto the streets of approximately 80 towns and cities on Wednesday, November 25. Workers from both the public and private sectors protested against further austerity and war spending. “We refuse to pay with our lives and incomes for involvement in war and the profits of business groups,” the All-Workers Militant Front (PAME) stated when announcing the strike. The strike call had already been launched during the dockworkers’ international day of action against the militarization of ports at the end of October. It is expected to ripple outward in the coming weeks, including during a new national mobilization on December 15. Read more: Dockworkers at 110 ports worldwide strike against war and genocide “Today’s strike shows that the policy that is crushing our lives, that brings yet another budget of profits and war, has an adversary: the organized labor movement, the collective action of workers, of struggling farmers, of the self-employed and of the youth,” PAME wrote. The union emphasized broad participation across sectors, from construction to public transport and administration. “Through persistent organizing in the workplaces, in the face of employer intimidation, blackmail and threats, the hundreds of strike decisions taken ‘from below,’ many by unions that have taken such a decision for the first time, show that ‘the new’ and hopeful in our lives will be born out of exactly this kind of action, multiplying the sites of struggle and demand.” Workers across sectors participated in the November 25 strike. Source: PAME/Flickr The strike in Greece comes as unions across Europe continue taking action against cuts to social security made in the name of militarization. Over the past weeks, mass demonstrations and industrial actions have taken place in Italy, Spain , France , and Belgium , all demanding more investment in social protection and labor rights. “In Greece, as in Italy, inadequate wages, the rising cost of living, job insecurity and deteriorating working conditions are affecting millions of people, whilst enormous resources are being channelled into rearmament and military spending,” the Italian grassroots union Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) wrote in a statement of solidarity with PAME. “War is not a prospect for the future of the people,” echoed the Trade Union Association of Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia from the Czech Republic . “It is death, destruction, poverty, and new opportunities for profit for the arms industry, while the working class always pays the price.”

articles.title: “Disaster Waiting to Happen”: Iowa Declares Emergency as U.S. Army Detonates 5 Tons of Lead Azide
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman. Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. The detonation will cause a massive blast that could send toxic lead dust spewing across communities, farmland, and potentially into the Mississippi River. The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time. Officials have recommended residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant to evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. Men are being told to — in this farmland area, to bring their cows inside. A number of farmers have said that’s impossible. Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, told a reporter he plans to go west to escape the toxic plume. JEREMY ATWATER : But now the winds are changing directions, and it’s going to blow directly south through our town, so I guess we’re going to head west instead. REPORTER : And what’s out west? Is it hotels? Or is it just — JEREMY ATWATER : Anything but the bomb. … My primary concern is a lot. I mean, nobody really knows. There’s never been a documented explosion like this, as far as I could find any doing my due diligence digging in the interweb. But it’s just going to be a big problem. It’s going to be a lot of lead poisoning going on. AMY GOODMAN : The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There’s no safe level of lead exposure. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women. The Army says the explosives, stored for decades in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, have deteriorated to the point that they could spontaneously explode. This is acting Army Secretary Adam Telle speaking at a press conference in Iowa Tuesday. ARMY SECRETARY ADAM TELLE : There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance. AMY GOODMAN : On Saturday, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option, a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Well, for more, we go to Lexington Park, Maryland, where we’re joined by Pat Elder, the founder of the group Military Poisons. He just wrote a piece headlined “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.” Pat Elder, welcome back to Democracy Now! Iowans are panicked. PAT ELDER : Thank you. AMY GOODMAN : They say they have gotten very little notice about what’s about to take place. If there are hills, they’re saying people are heading to the hills. But what do they do with their cows, those who are farmers? If you could start off by saying why you see this as a warning to the world? And how on Earth did this surprise this whole community, where the governor now has declared a disaster emergency in three counties? PAT ELDER : Well, thank you for having me, Amy. I appreciate it. We have to go back to the words of Thomas Jefferson, who wrote in the Declaration of Independence that we must be warned of usurpations by the federal government that will strip the liberties of individual states. And so, that’s what we see today. The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts and experts with the EPA and experts with the Applied Physics Lab, Johns Hopkins here in Maryland. There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen. And I feel sorry for the poor folks in Iowa, as I do for people around the world who suffer these same sorts of fates, because the United States Army does what it wants and has acted in a Neanderthal fashion with its detonation and supposed disposal of hazardous materials. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s talk about the effects — PAT ELDER : I think it’s — AMY GOODMAN : — of lead, Pat Elder. If you can talk about the health concerns for lead exposure, especially for children and fetuses? The New York Times says lead is a neurotoxin, and there are no safe levels for exposure. Can you take it from there? PAT ELDER : Well, I can, Amy. Thank you so much. We know, all the way from our experiences with leaded gas and lead paint, and the fiasco in Flint, Michigan — we have the clinical data — we understand that lead is a killer. It is a killer in the embryo. It is a killer for young children. And it is a killer for all of us. But the Army would pretend that this is not the case, because — well, because it’s very fond of lead in ammunition. And so, we look around the country, and we see where the Army has been absolutely irresponsible in the way that it handles lead. We look at Fort Ord in California, for instance, and entire sand dunes are loaded with lead, and campers are allowed to traipse. They built an entire campus at the University of California, Monterey Bay, over top of old Army buildings with lead pipes. The poor kids are drinking lead. The Army is irresponsible when it comes to lead all around the world. It has buried it, and it has — supposed to be following a process, that it does not follow, to safely dispose of lead. AMY GOODMAN : So, let’s — PAT ELDER : And I want to add, too — AMY GOODMAN : Go ahead. PAT ELDER : Yeah, thanks. Just, you know, we’re not just dealing with lead here. We’re dealing with lead azide. And the best way to put this into focus is that lead azide is the explosive that detonates a bomb. So, if we have a 2,000-pound bomb that is falling on Gaza, lead azide the size of a small pea is detonated, which then sends a tremendous blast into the bomb itself. So, it is the explosive agent. And this is the material the Army is getting ready to detonate. And so, we’re not just talking about lead itself. We’re also talking about contaminations like hydrogen cyanide and hydrazoic acid. These are deadly. They deprive the brain of oxygen. And this is what is getting unleashed on the people of Iowa. AMY GOODMAN : I want to ask you about that New York Times exposé on Saturday that may have surprised many, as so much of this has just crept up on them, the people of the community. It’s not as if this is a story that broke into the whole, you know, country. But they’ve been dealing with it for a while. Many residents did not know until the last few days what was about to happen. But The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option: a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded this contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Pat Elder, explain. PAT ELDER : Well, we have to go back to March of 2025 to fully understand what has transpired. The Army itself, along with experts from the EPA and experts with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab here in Maryland, sat down, and they all voted that it would be too dangerous to detonate these materials, and that the way to do it is to saturate the exterior of these barrels, and the interior of these barrels once they are opened, with a chemical compound that is made of sulfur in water. And so, we spray that over the barrels. And when the Army says, “Well, this is too dangerous,” MuniRem, the company behind this process, has said that it would use robots, as it has in decontaminating other Army ammunition sites. So, the entire process and the entire culmination in the Army deciding suddenly that they would go ahead and detonate this material is lunacy. And the idea that way back in August of 2025, we — the Army knew that there was a problem, and MuniRem knew there was a problem, and Johns Hopkins knew, and the EPA knew. The last people to find out are the people of Iowa and the people that live in the immediate area. They didn’t find out until last week. And that’s how the Army operates. AMY GOODMAN : Pat Elder, I want to thank you for being with us, founder of the group Military Poisons. We’ll link to your piece , “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.” Coming up, Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy. He just won the National Book Award for Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , but he wasn’t at the award ceremony. The U.S. denied ElGendy a visa. While he was a political prisoner in Egypt, starting when he was 17 years old, he published his writings in the Egyptian independent paper Mada Masr . Right now we are awaiting a court’s decision, an appeal of the government’s just closing down Mada Masr . We’ll go to Cairo, as well. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Massive Will” by Emel Mathlouthi, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. To see all the performances and interviews in our Democracy Now! studios of musicians and artists, go to democracynow.org .

articles.title: “Huna”: Egyptian Author Abdelrahman ElGendy on Prison, National Book Award & Being Denied U.S. Visa
articles.content: This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations. “It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.” We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr , whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown. “ Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr . “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

articles.title: Iran, Neoliberalism, Nihilism, and the Global Order A Conversation with Wendy Brown
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: Conducted in early 2026, on the eve of the assault on Iran by Israel and the USA, this interview with Wendy Brown explores the transformation of the state under finance capital and the intensification of social nihilism. Although publication was delayed due to the interviewer’s travel to Iran, Brown’s analysis of the “global construction” of the Iranian predicament and the “privatisation of the state” remains strikingly prescient and conceptually vital for understanding the current crisis. From the “equal right to inequality” to the extraction of profit from destruction in Gaza, the conversation offers a rigorous materialist map of the neoliberal ruins we inhabit Mohammad Hadi : Although the timing of this conversation coincides with the tragic situation in Iran and the killing of many innocent people – a disaster that casts a shadow over thought, or at least my own – I began this conversation with some difficulty. I have been grappling with a stifling force that shrinks the space for reflection. A voice from both inside and outside tells me that I should only think of what is happening in Iran. This position not only comes into contact with the logic of identity politics but also displays a harsh criticism: why, at this particular historical juncture, turn one’s attention instead to a discussion of neoliberalism? Wendy Brown : I don’t know if I can help you, but I am going to engage your question. To understand the predicament of Iran, one has to move outside of Iran and think about imperialism. We must look at least as far back as the US positioning itself in relation to the Shah as a puppet power, and a larger Middle East politics that has been negotiated and changed over the course of the Cold War and the post-Cold War period. To think about the extraordinary uprising in Iran of the past month – the tremendous courage and sacrifice so many Iranians made in struggling for an opening and a new arrangement of power – one is already forced to think about the global construction of the Iranian predicament. The Iranian situation is never just about Iran. The place of neoliberalism here is significant. There is nothing the revolution of neoliberalism did not touch; in the past fifty years, nothing on the globe has been unaffected by globalisation, deregulation, privatisation, and the aiding and abetting of corporate and finance capital. Neoliberalism brought a fundamental transformation of the international order, which we have recently seen brought to something of an end in the squaring off between China, Russia, and the US. We see an absolute indifference to the fates and conditions of everyone else and the resurrection of a “spheres of influence” foreign policy by the remaining hegemons. Neoliberalism matters as a way of understanding parts of what has happened to the global order and parts of what has happened in Iran itself: making life unaffordable, the economy tanking, and the currency in a mess. While it doesn’t explain everything, especially the specific timing of the uprising, it has intensified the immiseration of the Iranian people beyond the level of state repression or the enforcement of Islamic law. MH : You have argued that neoliberalism is not just an economic programme, but also a governing rationality that reshapes how we understand freedom, responsibility, and even ourselves as political subjects. How would you explain this broader project to someone encountering your work for the first time? WB : We need to offer recognition where it is due: this is an idea that Michel Foucault helped the world understand. Foucault grasped that neoliberalism was not just a set of economic policies – though it does comprise deregulation, privatisation of public goods, and stripping the welfare state. The important thing is that these policies are part of a larger order of political reason or political rationality. He helped us understand the shift from liberalism to neoliberalism as one involving a transformation of the state, society, and the individual subject. With neoliberalism, the state becomes a more overtly constructivist actor; it is turned to construct and support markets, not just to get out of the way like the “night watchman” state of classical liberalism. It is actively engaged in the facilitation of capitalist accumulation. Unlike the Keynesian or social state, which is redistributive, neoliberals wanted a state that would support capital with the recognition that capital does not run with ease by itself; it needs the support of political policy and legal codes. Furthermore, neoliberal reason involves an assault on the very idea of “the social”. Margaret Thatcher famously declared there is no such thing as society, and F.A. Hayek referred to the social as a “dangerous fiction”. Individual subjects are changed from citizens into bits of “human capital” in every aspect of their lives. We see young people preoccupied with rankings, ratings, and followers, which signifies a preoccupation with their ability to attract investors to themselves. This transformation breaks us up into individual entrepreneurial units that either sink or swim, as opposed to being gathered into a social whole. There were dimensions of this project that the original neoliberal intellectuals had not counted on. They did not anticipate the extreme inequality and precarity that would produce a highly activated, angry population – what we call populism on both the Right and the Left. They also did not count on financialisation – the growth of the finance sector at the expense of every other aspect of the economy. The final coup of neoliberalism was not just to privatise public goods, but to privatise the state itself. The financialisation of the state – the overtaking of the state by private finance – is the subordination of states to capital. The original neoliberals counted on the state being able to manage different aspects of markets to facilitate capital; they didn’t count on states being so overtaken by capital that they become the servants while finance is the master. This rationality gets into our heads; we think constantly about how to enhance our capital value and prevent its depletion. MH : Ideals such as freedom, tolerance, rights, and individual choice appear not only as democratic achievements but also as sites where power operates in subtle ways. How do these values become detached from democratic equality and redirected toward exclusion or authoritarian forms of politics? WB : One way to answer this is to note the extent to which neoliberalism has intensified a nihilism already developing in Western culture. Nihilism, theorised by thinkers like Nietzsche and Weber, suggests that, once science and reason displace the authority of God, you lose the fundamental foundations of values. Reason and science only explain how things work; they do not explain what to value. Neoliberalism puts this nihilistic project “on steroids” by claiming all there is to life is economic action. We are reduced to homo economicus across every aspect of life, from dating and mating to education and choosing friends. On a more specific level, consider the values of equality, liberty, and fraternity. Equality is reduced to the “equal right to win or lose in a market” – the equal right to inequality. Liberty becomes the right to do or say anything that enhances your competitive positioning, including the right to be insulting or egregious. Liberty is reduced to a private property right where you are the property. Fraternity simply doesn’t exist in a neoliberal order. The social contract, which says the government should assure minimal thresholds of survival and solidarity, goes away. Freedom, once understood as participation in popular rule, loses its political dimension. MH : I have been struck by the thought that neoliberalism is a great plunderer, but its theft is not limited to the rights of its own citizens. It operates through a profound deception: while it dispossesses its own citizens of welfare and rights, it presents a veneer of legitimacy elsewhere, promising “freedom” to other lands while actually expropriating the possibility of citizenship and democratic capacity. WB : If I understand your comment correctly, you are suggesting that under the guise of freedom, neoliberalism strips human beings of every other aspect of survival. The US experiment in Iraq is a superb example. After toppling Saddam Hussein, the effort to neoliberalise the country involved denationalising banks and making all of Iraq’s assets available for external investment and plunder. It was all done under the sign of freedom, but it intensified long-simmering conflicts, brought the Taliban to Iraq, and cast many Iraqis into poverty and death. Indebtedness is one of the great tricks of neoliberal austerity; it transforms regions into indebted ones from which they can never climb out, producing a desperate population that may turn to the right, the left, or simply submit. MH : In In the Ruins of Neoliberalism , you wrote that the neoliberal critique of social justice in the name of traditional moral norms has become “common sense”. Figures like Trump, Orbán, or Musk, and even Iranian monarchists, pursue a form of authority that promotes traditional values – family, hierarchy, masculinity – in constant interplay with the fluidity of the market. What does this coexistence between a rigid command and market fluidity mean to you? WB : This is an interesting problem because there has always been a strong tension between the right-wing endorsement of traditional values and the “free market”. Irving Kristol, a founder of neoconservatism, withheld a “third cheer” for capitalism because he understood it had a terrible effect on morality and tradition. Capitalism is an innovative, constantly destructive order. Today’s “postliberals” want to affirm capital while using the state to attenuate its effects. They use the state to support families, transform education toward tradition and away from critical thinking, and allow a post-secular religious order to unfold. You see this in Modi’s India, Orbán’s Hungary, and Iran. Orbán uses heavy statism to support a moral-theological project even as capitalism undoes it. Their task is to manage that contradiction – to use the state to offset capital’s effects and ward off reformers who challenge gender norms or reproductive freedom. Figures like Trump are manifestly immoral and non-religious, yet they speak the political discourse of tradition. This resonates with the Iranian diaspora, who may not be religious but stick to traditional values to ward off the perceived “wreckage” of modern life. MH : Neoliberal rationality systematically outsources political judgment and responsibility to market metrics and technocratic governance. I would suggest further that to preserve its legitimacy, this order also outsources its “negative residuals” – violence, failures, and ethical debts – onto other actors or distant abstractions. Morality itself is removed from the centre of political life and reassigned to distant humanitarian spectacles. WB : I wonder if “disavowal” is a better word. The quintessential example is the original neoliberal experiment in Chile. The tremendous violence – people being shot in stadiums – was disavowed by the “Chicago Boys” for years. Neoliberalism prefers “soft power” and managerial language, yet it engages in “slow violence” – sinking masses into despair or uprooting lives through industrial transformation. Neoliberalism has a language of intense disavowal, calling “hostile takeovers” “private equity” to make the takeover of housing and healthcare sound decent. This disavowal permits scapegoating; when life becomes unaffordable, people point to what is near, blaming immigrants, feminists, or elite politicians for their suffering rather than the takeover of buildings by private equity. MH : When it comes to violence, I still tend toward the word “outsourcing”. I am thinking of Mary Kaldor’s distinction between “old” and “new” wars, where conflicts are defined by fragmented constellations of state, non-state, and private actors. Violence is dispersed and contracted out. In Iran, the scale of war is effectively transferred to the people themselves. Civilians are mobilised through calls and incitements from outside – the US, Israel, or the son of the Shah – to go to the streets, which results in more repression. War is displaced onto intermediaries; populations and bodies carry the cost. WB : That is an interesting point. War is now disseminated throughout political and economic spaces; it is no longer just sovereign nation versus sovereign nation. We see this in trade and tariff wars that intermingle national security with economic advantage. There is a loss of boundedness between these spheres. I would add “terror” to this spectre of war. Protesters struggling against state power in both Iran and the US are declared “terrorists” by the very military enacting terror toward the people. The people are recast as illegal combatants. MH : Neoliberalism also appropriates perspectives that appear emancipatory. Some on the left emphasise horizontalist accounts of politics. Thinkers like Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri posit the end of sovereignty as if the age of governing authority is concluding. I regard their claim primarily as a description of what is happening under neoliberalism rather than a form of resistance. What do you think? WB : I completely agree. Sadly, both anarchism and horizontality, when closely read, are often effects of neoliberal discourse rather than resistances to it. Anarchy is essentially a version of the extreme neoliberal aspiration: no rules, no state, just a natural order emerging from individual actions. The “post-sovereign” fantasy is the original neoliberal fantasy: that capital moves freely while navigating a diminished sovereignty. Hardt and Negri would have to rethink their thesis today. Sovereignty is having a huge symptomatic expression as it goes down, seen in the repression of dissent by individual sovereigns. MH : Finally, neoliberalism can even derive benefit from failure, injustice, and terror. We see “predatory wolves” excited to rebuild the “Riviera of Gaza” out of a nightmare of destruction and genocide. Trump, for instance, refrains from direct war with Iran because he must first discern how to convert the circulating violence and fear into advantage. WB : Watching the “predatory wolves” so excited to begin rebuilding the “Riviera of Gaza” was a perfect expression of this. There was excitement about possible development opportunities coming out of that nightmare of genocide, ecocide, and scholasticide. Neoliberalism is exceptional at taking destruction and extracting the last bit of profitability from it. You see this in asset managers who get excited about driving industries into the ground to extract what they can in their death throes. Your description is poetic and unfortunately accurate. The only note of promise I want to end on is that a great many people in the world have had it with this mode of organisation and planetary destruction. You are seeing signs all over the place – not just a turn to fascism, but a turn to resistance and the building of futures that have a different order of things at their heart.
