articles.title: Japan to revise national security policy, weaken postwar non-nuclear commitments
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) claimed on Monday, November 23, that it will revise the country’s three security documents by the end of the year and possibly acquire nuclear-power submarines soon. Civil society groups on China and Japan have been opposing the decision, calling it a move towards remilitarization. They also claim such a move would be disastrous for regional peace and security and for the post-war regional order. Keitaro Ohno, a leader of the LDP and a member of Japanese parliament reportedly reiterated that Japan has rejected the proposal to get a nuclear-powered submarine in the wake of strong popular opposition and objections raised by China. He also claimed there is a consensus within the ruling coalition on the matter. The conservative LDP, along with the right wing Japan Innovation Party (JIP), holds a supermajority in the House of Representative (lower house) of Japan’s National Diet (parliament). On Friday, Japan’s civil society groups had submitted 47,000 signatures to the country’s Defense Ministry, urging it to abandon the plan to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and amendments in the security documents. Japan has also recorded several popular mobilizations against the Sanae Takaichi-led government’s moves to revise the three security documents, including its three non-nuclear principles, which prohibit its government from acquiring, producing, or introducing nuclear weapons. Still, reports indicate that the Japanese government is aiming to make changes in its National Security Strategy, one of the three security documents, within the next few months, to allow nuclear weapons to be brought in the country during an “emergency.” Civil society groups expressed concerns at the Takaichi government’s attempts to introduce nuclear weapons in the country even under this pretense, claiming it violates one of the three non-nuclear principles of not introducing the weapons. They claimed once Japan moves ahead with the acquisition it will fundamentally alter the country’s status from a non-nuclear weapons’ state to a nuclear weapons state and this will go against its stated responsibility to promote nuclear disarmament. Japan’s commitment to nuclear disarmament is rooted in the fact that it remains the only country in the world which has faced nuclear attacks. Impact on relations with China China has warned successive Japanese governments including Takaichi against any attempt to re-militarize the country claiming any such move would shake the balance in the region and will lead to instability and arms race. Read more: China urges Japan to abandon nuclear ambitions and respect international law China has demanded that the international community check the Japanese government to keep it from violating its commitments to the post-war order, drawing their attention to Japan’s imperial past and its devastating impact on all other nations in the region, including China. Though several Japanese governments in the last few years have expressed “revivalist” intentions and talked about re-militarization of the country, the Takaichi government has made significant efforts in that direction despite Chinese objections and risks of confrontation. Earlier this year, Takaichi even talked about military intervention in case China attempts to integrate Taiwan militarily. She made the comments despite a long standing Japanese commitment to “One-China” policy. China reacted strongly to her statement and demanded she apologize. However, Takaichi refused to apologize or withdraw her statement, which created prolonged diplomatic tension between the two countries. During last week’s visit to Shenzen, China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Summit (APEC) she, however, reaffirmed her government’s commitments to the 1972 Japan-China Joint Statement and four political documents signed by the two countries, indicating moderation. Reacting to her statement, Guo Jiakun, spokesperson of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said last week that Japan must fulfill its political responsibility and legal obligations towards China as described in the four documents – not just verbally but through “concrete action.” “For Japan, the pressing priority is to correct the erroneous words and moves on the Taiwan question, adopt a correct attitude on historical issues, and form an objective and rational perception on China,” Guo said.

articles.title: Iowa lead bomb: Abby Martin says the real threat is ‘your army’
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: The Pentagon is set to explode five tons of lead azide next to a small town in Iowa on Wednesday. Abby Martin says that’s the real threat to the homeland: “It’s not Iran dropping a dirty bomb on us. It’s your army.” Middletown and communities across the interstate fallout radius are bracing for the toxic contamination of homes, the country’s corn supply, and the Mississippi River, after Trump passed the buck to Iowa’s incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand and a federal appeals court greenlit the blast. Martin, the Empire Files journalist and director of Earth’s Greatest Enemy, joins Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra to expose the US military’s devastating environmental footprint, from toxic waste and PFAS contamination at bases across the country to the pollution and destruction left behind by US wars abroad. Martin says the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, an EPA Superfund site since 1990, is also “supplying arms to kill little girls in Gaza, in our name, with our tax dollars.” The tank shell that killed two ambulance paramedics attempting to rescue 6-year-old Hind Rajab was manufactured in Middletown. And the military industrial complex escapes accountability on the world stage, too: Martin slams the collapse of COP31 on Sunday – “What the hell are we doing? What are these conferences even about?” – and the exclusion of military emissions from climate reporting. Why does the world’s largest institutional polluter get a pass on the global climate debate? But Martin also points to a growing wave of grassroots resistance racking up wins. Communities across the US uniting in opposition to military bases and AI data centers are proof that militarism isn’t inevitable: “These are winnable fights.” Watch Abby Martin’s documentary Earth’s Greatest Enemy and learn more about her work with The Empire Files: https://empirefiles.tv/ Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Interviewer:] Thank you so much for having me, you guys. It’s amazing to be here. [Speaker 2:] It’s so great to have you on, Abby. Let’s start with the Iowa story before we get into some of the other stuff. The army is saying that this stuff is too unstable to move, so instead, they’re going to blow it up in place as the safest option. How does five tons of degrading explosive, first of all, sit in bunkers for decades if it’s so unstable? And why is the solution always to dump the risk on the people next door? What’s happening here? [Abby Martin:] Yeah, I mean, first of all, this was an entirely avoidable crisis. Blowing up 10,000 pounds of lead explosives is a deliberate choice. They could have chemically neutralized this stuff, the entire stockpile, without a single explosion months ago. According to internal documents from the New York Times, this was a deliberate choice to opt for the explosion. There’s no accountability or answer to why that was. They’re opting to unleash lead-laden explosives, a toxic plume over 120 miles of cornfield. Iowa is the largest corn-producing state in America. This corn is in most processed foods, most animal feed. It just shows how this institution does not care about the law or people’s lives. They didn’t even notify people until five days before the initial planned detonation, including Iowa officials. This is the Pentagon’s playbook wherever it operates. Every place it stores toxic or hazardous materials, it cannot be trusted. We’re talking about everywhere around the world. It defers maintenance for these aging stockpiles like in Red Hill, Hawaii. They wait for something catastrophic to happen. In Iowa, these barrels were sitting there for 20 years. Suddenly, overnight, they’re too dangerous to move. So, what do they do? I guess we just have to blow them up. They do not actually incorporate the costs to the environment or human health. For them, this is the most cost-effective thing. But again, it’s an emergency of their own making because of their own negligence and disregard. I just can’t wrap my mind around the fact that an industry with a budget of over a trillion dollars cannot incorporate a safe disposal mechanism for these toxic chemicals that it is constantly manufacturing. They just know that they can override local governments and do this kind of stuff anyway. [Interviewer:] Really sinister stuff there. This plant has been a Superfund site since 1990. Explosives turned up in local streams and groundwater, and the army had to hook nearby homes up to rural water. In your film “Earth’s Greatest Enemy,” you document this exact scenario and pattern. How typical is Middletown and what they’re facing today? [Abby Martin:] Shockingly, most Superfund sites in the US are either current military installations or have previously housed military use. This is completely routine practice for the world’s largest polluter. Twenty-five years ago, the US government called to halt the destructive and deadly practice of open burning and open detonation. The military, as it often does, just completely ignored this and continues to use open burning and open detonation as the routine practice to dispose of toxic and hazardous materials. Dozens of military sites around the country are openly burning and detonating hazardous waste and material. One of the most disturbing things about making the documentary was that everywhere you went that the military operates, you find the same exact story. Everywhere around the world that the US has a base, you find the same toxic legacy of environmental destruction. We’re talking about nuclear radiation, Agent Orange, and chemical testing. But it’s not just the legacy of all the testing up until now. Guam, for example, we went to Tarague Beach where the Air Force is detonating and open burning on ancient ancestral land that is a sea turtle habitat that the Chamorro people have used for generations. They’re doing it just willy-nilly. For years and years, they’ve had to be sued by the local EPA. This is where it gets really tricky because the EPA authorizes this stuff. The very organization that is tasked with protecting the environment is actually giving the army emergency measures and provisions to do these horrific planet-destroying activities on a regular basis. You look at PFAS contamination, this is the next looming health disaster around the country. Every single military base has PFAS contamination seeping out into the groundwater. When there could have been safe disposal, safe alternatives decades ago, they choose to do this. We know the toxic legacy in Iraq and Afghanistan. We know the ecocide being committed now. These are just munitions. This is the lead and toxic compounds from just munitions that are exploded in wartime. But it’s so important to know that this is happening in relative peacetime to maintain a global military arsenal. It requires an insane amount of chemicals to treat the equipment, to maintain the engine parts to be mission-ready. It’s incomprehensible the amount of pollution this is causing. I just want to give you one statistic. The DoD reports through its toxic inventory release that it dumps 28 million pounds of toxic waste into the environment annually in the US. This number does not include tons of unreported chemicals and it does not include overseas bases. So just imagine how much this is happening, how much we can’t quantify. Again, it’s all happening completely extra-legally by the same government agencies that are supposed to be protecting our land and our health. [Interviewer:] Just to follow up on that, Abby, another area you follow closely is what’s happening in Gaza. The Nation actually traced shell fragments from the ambulance where two Palestinian paramedics were killed while trying to rescue Hen Rajab back to the same plant in Iowa. Talk about that connection. [Abby Martin:] I don’t even want to really talk about the imperial boomerang because it makes it seem like these weapons weren’t tested here on Black and brown populations before they were exported to indigenous communities and in these sacrifice zones all around the world. But it is such a visceral example of how everyone’s connected. We are all victims of this military machine. The very plant that is about to drop a dirty bomb on American citizens and poison our corn and our food supply and the Mississippi River is the same plant that is supplying arms to kill little girls in Gaza in our name with our tax dollars. It is just such an extreme example of how the military-industrial complex hits here and abroad and how it does not care. We are all expendable in the eyes of this beast. [Interviewer:] It’s so crazy, that connection. I wanted to ask you about COP 31, which just collapsed after record overtime with no deal and not even the words fossil fuels in the draft. The US didn’t even send an official delegation this time. Military emissions are still voluntary to report, and the US has stopped reporting them altogether. Can these summits ever mean anything while the biggest polluter isn’t even on the table? Even when the US does take a seat at the table, they never discuss the US military as your film “Earth’s Greatest Enemy” points out. [Abby Martin:] This COP has really revealed the futility of these things. I think we need to wrap it up, guys. Let’s wrap up these global conferences and get serious because it’s just a waste of money. It’s for the ruling class to go and pat themselves on the back and rehabilitate their greenwashing efforts and the clean energy initiatives that they’re doing to maintain neoliberalism and global capitalism. It’s such a slap in the face. Some countries in the global south were saying, “We are held hostage by an oil mafia that is running the climate agenda.” It’s always been essentially a farce because you’ve had people like Al Gore leading the effort with carbon capture, which is really cartoonish. Are we really capturing carbon cumulatively? It does nothing. It’s just a way for them to continue to extract fossil fuel and prevent what we actually need to do, which is stop drilling, keep the oil in the ground. For the first time in 17 years, this was the first time that the climate conference ended without a deal. Trump stopped sending delegations altogether. They have completely pulled out of this entire conference. But you have the main oil producers like Russia, Saudi Arabia leading the opposition, and because every country has veto power, no one can come to a unanimous decision. For the second COP in a row, they have not only left out the transition away from fossil fuels off the table, they have failed to even mention the culprit of who is the main driver of the climate catastrophe, which is fossil fuels. It is just absolutely comical at this point. It’s always been a farce. You go back to the Kyoto treaty led by Bill Clinton, and the Pentagon paved the way to have military emissions be exempt. For the last 20-plus years, we have not even counted cumulative emissions. If we’re not actually counting emissions, and if you look at US-led emissions, it’s more than half the world’s nations combined. That’s not even counting the 5% NATO mandate that Trump just deployed. We’re not even counting emissions, right? And now we’re not even talking about fossil fuels. So what the hell are we doing? What are these conferences even about? This one didn’t even talk about reparations for the global south like they promised last COP, which they paved a bunch of the Amazon rainforest to just fly out delegates anyway. It’s disgusting and insulting that the world is burning down around us, and we don’t even have the courage to muster to utter who’s driving the damage and destruction. [Interviewer:] I highly recommend people who haven’t seen it really do check out your film because the confrontation you have questioning US officials about the emissions of the US military and it not being counted is incredible. They don’t have an answer because they are complicit in this. That COP was worthwhile for getting that on the record at the very least. [Abby Martin:] Yeah, incredible stuff there. Going back to the situation in Iowa, it’s a small town. Environmental groups and local officials temporarily pushed back. The detonation is scheduled for tomorrow, but they did force the army at one moment to back down three different times in the past week. What’s the lesson there for Middletown and anyone living next to a base? I think the lesson is community organization. Even though this looks like it will happen, we know that it will, despite community pushback. They put these plants where there’s a low density of human population, even though it will have widespread effects on human health and the contamination of our food. They’re still putting it in a town with a couple hundred people because they know there won’t be widespread community pushback or they can kind of operate extra-legally and override the local government there. What we’ve seen with the midterm sweep and especially with the data center moratoriums is how viscerally people are reacting against big tech and personifying the face of the military-industrial complex with these data centers. They are winning. It’s not just a repudiation of Trump. It’s a repudiation of this entire kind of war, the military-industrial complex, the war with Iran. People are synonymizing it like you said, the Hen Rajab connection. Gaza has been a catalyst in the connective tissue for people to really understand how this affects everyone, and they’re manifesting into these fights against data centers. We’ve seen the success stories all across the US. Data centers and the war with Iran were some of the main issues that people pointed to as why they came out and voted in the midterms. We’ve seen big broad coalitions building with those success stories being pushed back against the data centers. Whether it’s a base contaminating your water with forever chemicals or a data center trying to override the local community, these are winnable fights. Divesting your institutions from weapons contractors, defeating that inevitability of militarism and empire being a permanent state. Going back to COP where Nancy Pelosi said, “Yeah, well, you know, the military is the solution.” They’ve just basically hung their heads in shame and thrown their hands up and said the empire is the solution for the problems that it causes. We really have to push back against that kind of military mindset and figure out how we can reclaim our agency here and win. [Interviewer:] I want to broaden that out a bit, Abby, because we’re talking about the midterms. Democrats did win big because Trump’s agenda is just so unbelievably unpopular. But one thing that’s been so striking about this election cycle and the conversation in general is the way the issue of climate change has just dropped off as a topic. I can’t remember the last time I saw it even raised. I wanted to get your thoughts on that danger and that this really isn’t an issue that registers so much politically anymore, even as so many progressive ideas are becoming mainstream across the country. [Abby Martin:] I think it could be best articulated with just how immediate the measures are of relief for people in this country. You said it yourself in the previous segment. We’re talking about 60% or more of Americans who are literally surviving paycheck to paycheck. They have no savings in the bank if there’s an emergency. Bread on their table, gas in their tank, these things are so immediate. Yes, they can connect them to the war abroad. Yes, they can connect them to big tech and the control of the military-industrial complex, but it’s harder to resolve the immediate urgency of climate change. On top of that, it’s just kind of fallen to the periphery. What scares me is the fact that fewer Americans actually believe in man-made climate change now than they did five years ago. I honestly point to the culpability of the mainstream media, the corporate media that acts on behalf of these power brokers and oil companies. They are subsidized by the very same structures of power that we need to be holding to account for poisoning the planet. The big banks, the big oil companies. This is hugely problematic. You can see this displayed with Gaza. The fact that Americans don’t even know how many Palestinians versus Israelis have died. This is malpractice. This is a criminal component of the media that obfuscates the truth and the reality that should be displayed on our nightly news. The fact that the military is poisoning and killing us all. It’s not Iran dropping a dirty bomb on us. It’s your army. The one that we worship. The one that we praise at sporting events. This is the one that’s going to kill us and poison your family and your earth. I just point to the fact that Americans simply are not told, and the lack of political education is astounding when it should be on the nightly news. As the world continues to burn around us, as climate change becomes more visceral and immediate than ever, it should be incorporated into every single policy prescription. But I think we all know why it’s not. [Interviewer:] Well, on that note, Abby, we appreciate you so much. I want to once again encourage everybody. If you haven’t seen “Earth’s Greatest Enemy,” even if you think you know, you don’t know. It is such an eye-opening film and it speaks to basically everything we’ve talked about in a really important and impactful way. Go watch “Earth’s Greatest Enemy,” support Abby’s work. Abby, thank you so much for joining us. We appreciate you so much.

articles.title: Gaza declares epidemic alert after meningitis claimed 15 lives
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: On Tuesday, November 24, the Ministry of Health in the Gaza Strip declared an “epidemic alert” across all governorates, after 1,790 meningitis cases were recorded, adding that at least 15 people had died from the infectious disease. The ministry warned of an increase in fatalities due to meningitis, particularly among children. It attributed the surge in cases to the repercussions of Israel’s genocidal aggression against Gaza and its continued ban on the entry of medicine and other essential supplies into the war-ravaged territory. Read more: The daily reality of Israel’s mass extermination of life in Gaza The director general of the Gaza Health Ministry, Dr. Munir al-Bursh, told Al Jazeera that Israel’s genocidal aggression on the besieged Strip has poisoned the environment, citing a recent report published by Oxfam that addressed the crisis. “The [Israeli] occupation committed environmental war crimes in Gaza, destroying vital infrastructure across the Strip – including potable water networks and sewage pumping stations. With only 19% of Gaza’s sewage pumping stations remaining functional, existing water supplies contaminated by sewage, and a severe shortage of clean water for sanitation, the inevitable result is the outbreak of meningitis,” Dr. Munir said. The prominent Palestinian health official demanded that the international community fulfill its responsibilities and pressure Israel to allow the entry of desalination plants and necessary pumps into Gaza. Moreover, experts suggest that mass displacement resulting in overcrowded tents and schools has further exacerbated the meningitis outbreak, as Israel continues to hinder reconstruction efforts and restrict the entry of prefabricated homes and building materials. Meanwhile, the lack of essential nutrients, protein, and vitamins caused by the ongoing aid blockade has led to widespread malnutrition. This, in turn, has weakened immune defenses in infants and young children, sparking a surge in meningitis. Israeli assault leaves over 99% of Gaza environmentally contaminated, says Oxfam On Monday, November 23, a report titled “Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival” was released by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS). According to the findings in the report, Israel’s military onslaught has caused extensive environmental contamination throughout Gaza. Toxins that encompass heavy metals, explosive remnants, asbestos from demolished structures, dioxins, and biological hazards currently threaten the critical ecosystems upon which Gaza’s residents depend for their survival. The investigation shows how Israel’s widespread military operations have affected roughly 78% of Gaza’s territory, while spatial analysis indicates potential contamination across over 99% of the region. It also demonstrates that environmental pollution now poses a threat to almost the entire Strip. “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come. The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival,” Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar noted. “This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” Behar emphasized.

articles.title: La cumbre nuclear de Shenzhen
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: Read in English here El 19 de noviembre, el presidente Xi Jinping de China organizó una reunión con el presidente Vladimir Putin de Rusia y el presidente Donald Trump de los Estados Unidos. Se reunieron en Shenzhen al margen del foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC). La declaración final que emitieron contenía una frase muy contundente: “Una guerra nuclear no se puede ganar y nunca debe librarse”. Esta frase provino de tres de los países con armas nucleares más importantes del mundo, de los cuales solo uno – los Estados Unidos – había utilizado una bomba nuclear contra civiles (en Hiroshima y Nagasaki en 1945). Los demás países con armas nucleares (Francia, India, Israel, Corea del Norte, Pakistán y el Reino Unido) no cuentan con arsenales de la misma magnitud que los de los tres que se reunieron en Shenzhen, lo que significa que no tienen la capacidad para librar una guerra nuclear total; para la mayoría de ellos, las armas nucleares constituyen un elemento disuasorio contra la destrucción de su Estado por parte de otros. La declaración de estas tres potencias, por lo tanto, es indicativa del clima a favor de un nuevo acuerdo sobre el peligro y la futilidad de las armas nucleares. El primer tratado sobre el uso de armas nucleares se firmó el 1 de diciembre de 1959. Este Tratado Antártico prohibió las explosiones nucleares y el desecho de residuos radiactivos en la Antártida. Le siguió, el 5 de diciembre de 1963, el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de Pruebas Nucleares entre la URSS, los Estados Unidos y el Reino Unido. Este segundo tratado prohibía las explosiones nucleares en la atmósfera, en el espacio exterior y bajo el agua, mientras que permitía las pruebas subterráneas (estas fueron finalmente prohibidas por el Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares del 10 de septiembre de 1996, aunque las principales potencias nucleares aún no lo han firmado). A lo largo de los últimos sesenta y siete años, hemos sido testigos de un aumento de los tratados destinados a gestionar la presencia diabólica de las armas nucleares durante las primeras décadas; posteriormente, asistimos al colapso de todo el mecanismo de gestión nuclear. Ese mecanismo ha sido desmantelado pieza por pieza. La reunión de Shenzhen es la primera en muchos años que retoma el discurso sobre el peligro de una guerra nuclear y todas las personas amantes de la paz deberían aprovecharla como punto de partida. El colapso de la gestión de las armas nucleares El 5 de febrero de 2026 expiró el Nuevo Tratado de Reducción de Armas Estratégicas (Nuevo START). Firmado en 2010 y prorrogado en 2021, este tratado había restringido las fuerzas nucleares estratégicas desplegadas por los Estados Unidos y Rusia y había establecido mecanismos de verificación. Es el último de los tratados que regulan los arsenales de armas nucleares de los Estados poseedores de armas nucleares en expirar. Actualmente no existen límites numéricos vinculantes para los arsenales de armas nucleares. En respuesta a ello, el secretario general de la ONU, António Guterres, dijo : “Por primera vez en más de medio siglo, nos enfrentamos a un mundo sin límites vinculantes para los arsenales nucleares estratégicos”. Sería inexacto afirmar que ya no queda ningún acuerdo sobre armas nucleares. El Tratado de No Proliferación Nuclear sigue vigente, al igual que otros tratados y obligaciones en materia nuclear. El peligro específico radica en que los dos Estados que poseen los arsenales más grandes (los Estados Unidos y Rusia) ya no operan bajo un límite bilateral vinculante para sus fuerzas nucleares estratégicas. Las garantías de moderación no pueden sustituir a las inspecciones, los intercambios de información, las definiciones acordadas y los límites exigibles. Los entendimientos políticos pueden desaparecer con un cambio de gobierno o un deterioro en las relaciones. Es por eso que la declaración de Shenzhen es significativa, pero solo si permite reconstruir un nuevo tratado entre estos países. El historial de lo que se ha perdido da que pensar: Primero. El Tratado sobre Misiles Antibalísticos (ABM), firmado en 1972, limitaba los sistemas de defensa antimisiles y ayudó a afianzar la relación estratégica entre Washington y Moscú. Los Estados Unidos se retiró el 13 de junio de 2002, cuando el presidente estadounidense George W. Bush decidió aprovechar la debilidad temporal de Rusia para promover los objetivos del poder estadounidense. Independientemente de la limitada promesa que se hiciera respecto a la defensa antimisiles, el abandono de las restricciones negociadas alentó a los adversarios a buscar nuevos medios para superar esas defensas. El gasto militar, un desperdicio de riqueza social, comenzó a dispararse. Segundo. El Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio, firmado en 1987, eliminó los misiles lanzados desde tierra de los Estados Unidos y la Unión Soviética con alcances entre 500 y 5,500 kilómetros. Washington se retiró del tratado el 2 de agosto de 2019, cuando el presidente Trump decidió presionar aún más para obtener ventajas de los Estados Unidos frente a Rusia. Toda una categoría de armas, que en su momento se había eliminado mediante negociación, volvió a formar parte de la planificación militar. Esta retirada acorraló aún más a Rusia y provocó la invasión del este de Ucrania. Estos dos ejemplos son la culminación de años de erosión en varios ámbitos del control de armamentos. Sin embargo, son los tratados más significativos que se han dejado de lado y, por lo tanto, han sumido al mundo en una nueva carrera armamentista, en particular una nueva carrera de armamentos nucleares. Estos acuerdos fueron producto del temor y del cálculo político. Eran necesarios para comprender que la inseguridad de un adversario podía convertirse en una catástrofe para todos. En ese sentido, las inspecciones y las restricciones funcionaban como medidas de fomento de la confianza a pesar de los desacuerdos. Su anulación ha restablecido una peligrosa dependencia de las evaluaciones de amenazas, las estimaciones de inteligencia y el criterio de los líderes que actúan bajo presión. En Shenzhen, los tres líderes no anunciaron reducciones, acuerdos de verificación ni un calendario para las negociaciones, pero han establecido una apertura política a través de la cual se podría reconstruir una agenda de paz. La participación de China agrega una dimensión importante, ya que Pekín no ha sido parte en la mayoría de estos tratados bilaterales. Un marco duradero debe abordar las preocupaciones de seguridad de Pekín, así como las de Washington y Moscú. La humanidad no puede permitirse descartar una oportunidad de negociación solo porque no se llegue a un acuerdo. La ausencia de Europa La ausencia de Europa en la reunión de Shenzhen es notable. En lugar de aceptar la distensión que podría resultar de la reunión en China, los líderes europeos se reunieron en Berlín para una reunión de la “Coalición de los Dispuestos”. Este nombre, “Coalición de los Dispuestos”, proviene de una plataforma desarrollada por el político británico retirado Keir Starmer en marzo de 2025, con el propósito declarado de que los líderes europeos apoyaran al ejército de Ucrania. Si en Shenzhen las tres grandes potencias hablaron de su preocupación por la guerra nuclear y la guerra en general, en Berlín los europeos hablaron de un aumento del gasto militar, de entregas de armas y de una campaña de mayor presión contra Rusia. Los miembros de la Coalición reafirmaron el compromiso de aportar 70 mil millones de euros en equipo militar, asistencia y capacitación para Ucrania en 2026, con un apoyo al menos equivalente en 2027. Propusieron una mayor presión económica sobre Rusia y discutieron la creación de una fuerza multinacional liderada por Europa, con el respaldo de los Estados Unidos, que operaría tras un alto el fuego. Estos compromisos ampliaron la infraestructura material de la confrontación. Shenzhen se centró en la desescalada a través del diálogo, mientras que Berlín puso firmemente sobre la mesa el tema de la escalada de los compromisos militares. Las declaraciones de los líderes europeos sobre el gasto militar se produjeron mientras sus propias poblaciones salían a las calles para condenar la agenda de austeridad que empobrecería aún más a Europa y la haría más insegura. No hubo ninguna mención pública a estas protestas, ni tampoco se reconoció que su agenda cuenta con un apoyo público muy bajo. La oposición a la agenda de aumento del gasto militar y mayor austeridad social alcanza el 63% en Italia, el 59% en Austria, el 56% en Alemania y el 55% en Estonia. La declaración en sí misma es anodina: solicita un mayor gasto militar y concesiones de parte de Rusia, pero no detalla un plan amplio para la seguridad europea. Toda la agenda se basa en la dependencia de Europa respecto a Washington en cuanto a capacidades militares cruciales y acceso diplomático. Esto hace que la agenda de Berlín sea totalmente insostenible. Agenda del BRICS+ La apertura de nuevas negociaciones para el control de las armas nucleares reviste especial importancia para la agenda del BRICS+. Los países ajenos a los principales bloques militares sufrirían consecuencias devastadoras a causa de una confrontación que ni iniciaron ni controlan. Su interés en reducir el peligro nuclear es directo, razón por la cual deberían presionar para que se entablen negociaciones en lugar de dejar el tema en manos de una conversación exclusiva entre las potencias más grandes. China y Rusia asistieron a Shenzhen en calidad de Estados nacionales. Su participación no les otorgó un mandato para negociar en nombre de todo el Sur Global. La prueba está en si su diplomacia crea un mayor margen para que otros países persigan el desarrollo, el comercio y políticas exteriores independientes. Una menor confrontación podría abrir ese espacio; un acuerdo que proteja únicamente los privilegios de los Estados poderosos limitaría su potencial. El BRICS+ ya ha vinculado el desarme a su agenda práctica de desarrollo. Los recursos consumidos por las carreras armamentistas no están disponibles para la salud pública, la vivienda, la restauración ecológica y la inversión productiva. Sus instituciones pueden ampliar el acceso al financiamiento, mientras que sus miembros exigen que las potencias nucleares cumplan con sus responsabilidades. La iniciativa del Nuevo Banco de Desarrollo de otorgar préstamos en las monedas nacionales de los miembros ilustra una vía para aumentar las opciones económicas de los países. En la 19.ª Cumbre del BRICS+, que se llevará a cabo en China, es probable que se discuta más a fondo la cuestión de la disyuntiva entre el desarrollo y la guerra. La importancia de Shenzhen radica en la posibilidad que ha reabierto. Tres potencias nucleares reconocieron un peligro compartido en un momento en que han desaparecido las restricciones vinculantes. La tarea ahora es hacer que ese reconocimiento se traduzca en hechos concretos: negociaciones, verificación, límites y reducciones. La humanidad necesita un movimiento internacional lo suficientemente fuerte como para insistir en que el próximo anuncio se refiera a armas retiradas y acuerdos firmados, en lugar de otro presupuesto destinado a preparar una guerra de la que ninguna sociedad puede sobrevivir. Vijay Prashad es un historiador y periodista indio. Es autor de cuarenta libros, entre los que se incluyen Balas de Washington, Una estrella roja sobre el Tercer Mundo, Las naciones oscuras: una historia del Tercer Mundo; Las naciones pobres: una posible historia del Sur Global y How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, escrito con Grieve Chelwa. Es el director ejecutivo de Tricontinental: Instituto de Investigación Social , corresponsal jefe de Globetrotter, y editor en LeftWord Books (Nueva Delhi). También ha hecho apariciones en las películas Shadow World (2016) y Two Meetings (2017). Este artículo fue elaborado por Globetrotter y No Cold War .

articles.title: Israeli forces raid Al-Ama’ri Refugee Camp, detain dozens of Palestinians
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: On Monday, November 23, the Israeli military stormed Al-Ama’ri refugee camp in Al-Bireh city in the central occupied West Bank. During the hours-long raid, Israeli forces converted the Al-Ama’ri Youth Center, alongside several residential homes, into temporary detention and field interrogation sites. They also damaged the facilities of the center. 30 Palestinians were briefly detained and interrogated after their homes were raided, but were released before the military left the camp. However, one Palestinian young man was arrested in the assault, during which stun grenades and tear gas were fired. Since January 2025, the Israeli military has intensified its campaigns against refugee camps across the West Bank, considering them bases for resistance groups in the occupied territory. These campaigns resulted in 102 fatalities , including 21 children. They also displaced over 34,000 Palestine refugees, among them 12,000 children, from Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams refugee camps. Furthermore, the Israeli army issued demolition orders for 514 buildings, according to a report published by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in September, 2026. On November 17, 2026, Israeli authorities issued order No. 123/26 , authorizing the seizure of neighborhoods and road networks in Tulkarm and the nearby neighborhood of Dhannaba for “military purposes.” The order, which encompasses Tulkarm Refugee Camp, is valid until December 31, 2028, raising acute concerns that Israel intends to permanently displace the residents, who fled the camp as a result of the previous military campaign.
